This note provides an exploration of certain properties and characteristics of these conversions, including their relationships with other subspaces such as the classical group's invariant subspaces and the characteristic polynomials associated with the symplectic matrix.

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes a layered graph representation to suggest entities connected to a given starting point. The underlying concept is that when navigating through an entity, a user typically moves in a directional, hierarchical manner, mirroring the structure of Wikipedia's category system. To incorporate this behavior, the proposed approach builds a layered graph by assigning entities a certain number of possible "steps," reflecting their position in the Wikipedia taxonomy. This feature enables the implementation of a "distance" filter to limit recommendations based on the desired level of abstraction, effectively preventing recommendations that involve excessive "hops" between entities. Experimental results show that this approach achieves a more human-like entity recommendation, outperforming traditional methods in terms of accuracy and user evaluation.

Organ procurement agencies and online platforms that facilitate kidney exchanges often employ a variety of algorithms to optimize the number of transactions. However, the success of these algorithms relies on the ability to accept or reject proposed matches on the spot. To investigate this phenomenon, we develop an optimal decision-making framework that considers the highest achievable number of transactions when matches can be accepted or rejected. Our analysis reveals that the best outcome is achieved by accepting any proposed match that adds at least the minimum of two times the number of living donors who have found a match, minus one, as well as the number of recipients who have a living donor. We also examine the behavior of specific algorithms within this framework and the implications of our findings on kidney exchanges with altruistic donors.

This paper provides an overview of a specific graph connection called implicit connections, which are based on the ability of nodes to collect and make decisions based on partial information about their neighbors. This ability enables certain nodes to make equivalent decisions as those nodes with direct connections. As a result, implicit connections can represent a broader range of preferences and enable the reduction of complex connections into more manageable ones. This reduction can lead to significant improvements in modeling, such as increased resilience in dynamic scenarios and more accurate modeling with incomplete information. Additionally, implicit connections enable the use of established methods for analyzing complex connections that are otherwise intractable.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive examination of the capabilities of word embeddings, specifically in relation to the Loughran-McDonald's dictionary and polarity measures. Our analysis involves an initial training phase and a series of tests. During training, 12 different types of word embeddings are tested on their ability to distinguish between opposites listed in the dictionary. The results show that all the tested word embeddings can accurately identify the opposites. Nevertheless, when assessing the associations between words and their implied financial health indicators, our findings reveal a lack of consistency across the different embeddings. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that many of these implications are based on common word patterns rather than unique characteristics of financial text. In contrast, our findings indicate that neural-based sentiment analysis models are capable of accurately capturing the nuances of financial text. In addition, our analysis highlights the limitations of the Loughran-McDonald's dictionary and polarity measures, which may be too broad and are likely to be refined in the future.

This article proposes a novel waveforming technique that leverages a single carrier or a single spatial stream to provide maximum efficiency in both energy and data transmission. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we develop a single-carrier and a multi-carrier OFDM system that utilize a single antenna and multiple antennas respectively. Numerical results show that our proposed systems achieve significant gains over conventional OFDM systems in terms of sum rate and total transmitted power.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

In the realm of linguistic theory, particularly relevant to the context of this research is the concept of the "language network" - a tool used to visualize the structure of language based on the co-occurrence of syntactic patterns. Building upon this foundation, our study introduces a novel approach to interpreting unary connectives (negation and existential quantification) within this framework. We've developed an initial method for incorporating these operators into the language network, drawing from the principles of categorial type theory and the syntax of feature structures. This approach involves designating a specific type for the context that each expression is predicated upon, achieved by introducing the concept of "spin" - a contextual frame that identifies the type of the context. We've also explored a more nuanced understanding of "existence claims" by incorporating the context type into the type of the statement itself, enabling the distinction between assertions that make a general claim and those that are merely stating the existence of something.

In contrast to output-based assessments, where behavior is evaluated through performance metrics like accuracy or policy effectiveness, a more nuanced understanding emerges when analyzing behavior in multiplayer strategic situations. Here, the focus shifts on understanding why specific actions are taken, given their implications on both private and common payoffs. This study proposes a novel approach called Explainable Equilibrium Learning (EEL), which employs a combination of neural networks and reinforcement learning to train agents to follow a equilibrium strategy that incorporates the underlying decision-making process. This model is tested in various multiplayer settings with mixed-strategy equilibria, and its performance is compared to non-learned control methods. The results show that EEL can effectively learn to follow the desired equilibrium behavior and, more notably, the underlying exponential family distribution.

An analysis of a stochastic SIR epidemic model is conducted, where individuals on a random geometric graph connect to a fixed number of neighbors. Upon infection, these connections are replaced with new random links. The model is studied on a variety of graphs, including those with increasing connectivity, and the impact of the random link additions is compared. The goal is to understand how the number of new connections affects the spread of disease and the final population outbreak size. The analysis is facilitated by calculating the expected number of new connections and the efficiency of these links in preventing further transmission. The results show that in some cases, the added connections can actually increase the spread of disease and outbreak size, which may seem counterintuitive. However, it is demonstrated that this occurrence is not uncommon in epidemic spreading scenarios. The added connections enable the transmission of the disease to individuals who would otherwise have isolated (immediately) after infection. The efficiency of these links is shown to depend on the power law exponent of the graph, and specific conditions are identified for which the original connections reduce the spread of disease. The results also indicate that in some situations, the most effective strategy to prevent the spread of disease is not to isolate infected individuals or to vaccinate a random sample of the population, but rather to target a smaller number of key individuals whose connections would otherwise significantly contribute to the further transmission of the disease.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally isometric to a non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator and a non-zero eigenvalue.

A theoretical interpretation framework is proposed to facilitate the interpretation of data through probability density functions, thereby enabling an effective integration of experimental and theoretical data within the context of a global analysis. This interpretation framework is integral to the proposed extension of the existing group's analysis tasks, which includes the development of predictive models and the optimization of searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents often utilize experience replay to retrain the neural network policy. The standard experience replay method simply resamples episodes at a fixed rate, but this technique has been found to be less effective when the variance of rewards and state values is high. To address this limitation, a new variance-reducing experience replay algorithm has been developed, which incorporates two key components to enhance the effectiveness of policy optimization. Firstly, the algorithm adapts the sampling rate of episodes based on the estimated variance of rewards and state values, ensuring that episodes with low variance are sampled more frequently. Secondly, the algorithm incorporates a clipping mechanism to prevent the overestimation of action values and the subsequent increase in variance. The proposed algorithm is compared to several state-of-the-art baseline algorithms in two challenging benchmark tasks, and the results show a significant improvement in performance.

I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile C++11/14/17 template library that makes available a wide range of useful tools for manipulating polynomial-like objects, specifically designed for efficient use in quantum physics applications. Additionally, libcommute provides a comprehensive set of features for creating Hamiltonian classes and a user-friendly interface for developing exact diagonalization codes. With its customizable algebra definitions and domain-specific dialect, libcommute enables users to define custom Hamiltonian classes and perform diagonalization computations on various mathematical domains, including, but not limited to, integers, rational numbers, and complex numbers. Furthermore, libcommute provides an intuitive dialect called pycommute, which allows users to define algebraic structures and exact diagonalization problems using a Python language that can be seamlessly linked with the C++11/14/17 template library.

Establishing the nature of superconductivity in iron-based superconductors has been a challenging task. To address this, a study on the (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$  compound has been conducted to examine the electronic structure and superconducting gap structure. A notable discrepancy in previous measurements was identified or a need for further investigation in the results of certain spectral and superconducting gap features obtained from the data. To resolve this, a more detailed analysis of the experimental data was performed. The results showed that the superconducting gap structure in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ is more complex, exhibiting a nodal feature at the M point in the Brillouin zone. This finding is consistent with the results of first-principle calculations, suggesting that the superconducting pair function in this compound has an s$^{±}$-wave symmetry. The complexity of the superconducting gap structure in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ has significant implications for understanding the mechanism of superconductivity in this material.

Two new equations have been presented, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization equation, which both relate Gaussian Grassmann fields to arbitrary quadratic fields. A distinction between these equations has been identified, depending on whether a specific matrix is reflective or not. The connection between the equations has been explored for specific quadratic fields, including those from the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation itself, as well as Skew-Schur decomposition. The difference in the equations impacts their application in supersymmetric quantum field theories, particularly in the extraction of physical information from the partition function.

Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
were produced by the ATLAS experiment and yielded 3.69 ± 0.41 (stat.) ± 0.44 (syst.) 
pb^-1 of signal after accounting for trigger, reconstruction, and misidentification 
of background events. The measured value of $A_0$ was found to be -0.32 ± 0.43, 
with the standard model predicting a value of 0.44 for this asymmetry. Due to 
experimental limitations, particularly related to the forward reconstruction of 
charged leptons, the precision of this measurement is currently impeded.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the magnetic properties of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices at varying temperatures and with different nickel-neon interlayer spacings. Using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR, we found that the correlation length of magnetic interactions in LaNiO$_3$ can be significantly influenced by its interface with LaAlO$_3$. However, this influence diminishes as the nickel-neon interlayer spacing increases, likely due to reduced electron transfer between LaNiO$_3$ layers. Our findings also reveal that the spin-lattice relaxation mechanism switches from a direct Heisenberg interaction-dominated process at higher temperatures to a more orbital-correlated process at lower temperatures. This orbital-correlated process is anticipated to be more prevalent across the LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ interface.

Our MultiTalk dataset is an extensive dialogue testbed that incorporates a wide range of topics and categories. Unlike other datasets that focus on straightforward conversations, MultiTalk includes complex topics with many branches, making it challenging for conversations to explore the subject in depth. The dataset consists of 12 categories, encompassing 128 subtopics, and includes 125K training examples and 1.25K evaluation examples. Our findings reveal that models excel at initiating brief, straightforward conversations but struggle to engage in more complex conversations. Despite achieving high scores in individual subtopics, our research discovered a significant disparity between training and performance in dialogue contexts. To improve the state-of-the-art in dialogue, we discovered that a crucial factor is maintaining diversity in a branch. Our study shows that incorporating explicit diversity goals into training conversations leads to more varied and coherent turns of speech.

Our research is centered on a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) system that incorporates intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) to maximize ergodic throughput in a frequency-nonselect fading environment. To account for practical applications, we adopt a stochastic geometry approach, modeling IRS phase-shifts using uniform distribution and approximating complex reflection coefficients with real-valued equivalents. Utilizing the bound of approximated complex reflection coefficients and the uniform distribution of phase-shifts, we derive the probability distribution of the received signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and subsequently the ergodic throughput of the system. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of spatial correlation, IRS phase-shift distribution, and reflector size on the ergodic throughput. Numerical simulations validate our analytical findings.

We introduce a new set of modified gravity simulations that are fast, comprehensive, and applicable to a wide range of scenarios. These simulations are based on a variety of configurations that cover multiple degrees of freedom and non-dynamical parameters. They are specifically designed to support the GCOLA gravity simulation toolkit. Our simulation suite, which is called FastLA, offers a range of options that can simulate a range of gravitational phenomena, from weak-field interactions to strong-field gravitational waves. FastLA includes modifications to the movement of particles, gravitational waves, and black hole dynamics. It also includes corrections for the energy released during the merger of two objects and the subsequent movement of the resulting gravitational waves. FastLA can simulate a range of conformal coupling models, including those proposed in the general relativistic hydrodynamics framework. It can simulate simulations with up to a billion particles at a speed that is 100 times faster than typical N-body simulations.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source platform that transforms MediaWiki into a versatile tool for creating interactive knowledge graphs and collaborative projects. Developed by the University of Oxford's Nuffield Department of Orthopaedic Engineering and supported by the Oxford Centre for Innovation, WorkingWiki aims to facilitate teamwork and research by providing a powerful combination of features that include customisable workflows, statistics, query languages, and file management. By building upon MediaWiki's robust features and vast ecosystem of extensions, WorkingWiki effectively bridges the gap between research collaboration and open knowledge, encompassing uses cases such as semantic knowledge bases, customised databases, and integrated project management systems.

This study undertakes an active flame model based on linearized Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, incorporating heat release rate oscillations to replicate a stoichiometric methane-air jet flame subject to transverse harmonic pressure disturbances. The model is a advanced active flame model that utilizes a 2D beam representation to mimic flame dynamics and is particularly effective in identifying how transverse pressure disturbances impact flame instability. This model is a sophisticated expansion of previous work by Jiang et al. and is validated using direct numerical simulation data from the same research group, with excellent results obtained for strain rates up to 20 times the natural vortex shedding frequency. However, slight discrepancies were observed for higher frequency scans due to the influence of vortex-vortex interactions. This model is then applied to examine the influence of acoustic forcing on flame stability, revealing a subcritical super-stable regime existing between the Rayleigh-B\'enard instability boundary and the natural vortex shedding frequency. The natural vortex shedding frequency is determined by the beam's natural frequency divided by 20, with the flame exhibiting high amplitude oscillations at frequencies significantly higher than this value as a result of nonlinear behavior.

We've discovered a previously overlooked phenomenon in the oscillations of stars: there's a specific mode of vibration where a topological phase transition occurs as the strength of magnetic field variations changes. Using a method that accurately accounts for the interactions between different vibration patterns, we simulated the effects of a strong magnetic field on the oscillations of a star in various stages of evolution. The simulations revealed that the topological phase transition is a persistent feature of stellar vibrations, influenced primarily by the star's core density rather than its overall mass or other characteristics. The unique properties of this topological mode make it potentially identifiable through seismic analysis of stellar magnetic fields, which could provide valuable insights into the internal structure of stars.

We present a novel, universally applicable method to locate synchronized clusters and traveling chimeras in networks of coupled oscillators. Our method is precise, efficient, and robust to variations in parameter values. Unlike existing approaches, our method can discover dynamic states such as traveling chimeras without relying on the computation of Lyapunov exponents or top Lyapunov vector. Instead, we use a straightforward, network-independent algorithm based on the degree of connectedness of the phase space. This algorithm identifies and tracks clustered and traveling solutions in one dimension, as well as in higher-dimensional spaces. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using a specific example of a spiking neural network, a key area of study in neuroscience.

In certain two-dimensional lattice gases such as the extended-Hubbard and t-J models, effective quantum spin models like Shastry-Sutherland and doped antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models arise depending on the balance between hole movement and on-site and inter-site interactions. For these systems at half-filling, increasing inter-site interactions causes a transition from Mott-insulating to superconducting behavior, ultimately leading to a critical point where the inter-site interaction dominates. This study investigates the impact of inter-site interactions on one-dimensional lattice gases, specifically the Hubbard and Bose gases. It finds that in two dimensions, such interactions can give two-dimensional lattice gases the same properties seen in one-dimensional systems, driving the systems towards clustering rather than condensation. It also discovers that this effect can give one-dimensional lattice gases with condensation a two-dimensional counterpart in the form of clustering.

We investigate how neutrinos interact with ultralight scalar dark matter within the framework of the Standard Model. By considering the interaction mediated by a heavy particle, such as a Higgs boson or a heavy neutrino, we derive a relevant operator that could lead to significant lepton number violating processes, including the hypothetical $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay. To prevent this process from conflicting with experimental limits, we impose constraints based on the required parameter combinations, which involve the ultralight dark matter mass, its coupling to neutrinos, the neutrino mass, and the primordial neutrino abundance. To avoid conflicting with existing $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay limits, we find that the ultralight dark matter mass cannot exceed $10^{-12}$ eV, assuming a direct coupling between neutrinos and dark matter. This constraint also implicates the neutrino mass, which cannot exceed $0.1$ eV. Additionally, we find that the model is consistent with the observed large-scale structure of the universe, but may conflict with small-scale structure observations.

The unexplored nature of ultra-high energy photons above $10^{18}$ eV complicates the understanding of cosmic ray phenomena. While purely theoretical models exist, they fail to account for the lack of such photons in observational data. A new approach, based on constant photon flux density, has been found to align with experimental limits. Assuming isotropy, this model predicts the probability of photon-proton interactions resulting in cosmic ray events with kinked and bent trajectories. It also provides the probability distribution of photon energies observed in the cosmic ray flux, which is compared to experimental data on the PMSSM flux multi-component structure.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a physical concept that views gravity as a nonlocal phenomenon, meaning its effects rely on the history of spacetime events. This paper presents nonlocal gravity as a response to external curvature fields, analogous to how electromagnetism responds to electric and magnetic fields. A key difference is that nonlocal responses are history-dependent, linking nonlocality to noncausality. Nonlocal gravity is described by a constitutive relation that connects nonlocal electric and magnetic curvature tensors to their respective causal sources. This relation is a fundamental equation that defines nonlocal gravity within the framework. Nonlocal gravity theory offers a constitutive nonlocality perspective that is distinct from geometric and causal nonlocality perspectives. Furthermore, nonlocal gravity can be represented by a nonlocal action principle, resulting in field equations that include nonlocal curvature terms. This approach may provide a constitutive nonlocality perspective for other noncausal phenomena.

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. As such, update conflicts pose a significant challenge that must be managed to maintain consistency. As the scale of the system increases, the likelihood of conflict-starvation attacks also grows, making it essential to incorporate timeout-based specifications into data updates. To address these challenges, this paper presents a design framework called Remove-Win that produces conflict-free, specification-respecting, and timeout-safe replicated data structures. Using this framework, we designed a particular replicated data structure called the Remove-Win Counter, which meets these criteria and outperforms other comparable counter implementations in terms of update latency.

To gain a deeper understanding of genome-wide association studies and genomic data, we integrated two sources of information related to 18 human traits. We combined GWAS data with genomic functional characteristics across all human genes, using a comprehensive collection of data that includes gene expression levels from various tissues, binding sites for 92 different transcription factors, and genomic features such as gene length and position on chromosomes. We applied statistical methods to identify associations between GWAS hits and genomic functional characteristics, mapping the connections of each protein to specific genes and corresponding genomic features. The results showed significant differences in the frequency of connections between GWAS hits and protein interaction networks. Furthermore, we observed variations in the prevalence of genes with binding sites for transcription factors across the 18 traits, with some traits targeting a higher number of genes based on their specific characteristics, such as gene length, position on chromosomes, and expression levels in various tissues. We also explored the relationship between GWAS hits and genomic functional characteristics at a finer grain, examining the connections between each protein and specific genes, as well as genomic features such as gene length and position on chromosomes. We made these findings publicly available through an interactive web page, allowing users to easily access and compare the results for each trait.

This paper discusses the concept of minor systems, a new approach to understanding hadron collisions within the QCD framework. Unlike the standard leading-twist approximation, the minor systems framework considers all possible relations between partons and jet momenta, organizing them into a comprehensive set of variables. This approach reveals a fundamental connection between hadron collimation, jet deflection, and jet momentum, and shows how a single parameter, characterizing the collimation or deflection, determines the properties of jets and hadrons. The minor systems formalism offers a new statistical interpretation, where the hadron distribution is essentially a sum over jet distributions, and provides an explanation for phenomena through jet coherence, in addition to predictions for observables like jet shapes, boson-jet imbalance, and Bose-Einstein correlations within jets. The theoretical foundation involves the collinear and soft-fudge approximations, and the use of the light-cone wave function, but the formalism bypasses the direct parton-to-parton comparison often associated with leading-twist analyses.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way that contain a neutron star have shown that the accretion processes around these stars are likely powered by the spin of the neutron star. However, to confirm this, it is essential to determine the fraction of these systems that exhibit transient behavior. Transient duration is linked to the neutron star's recycling efficiency, which in turn affects the Alven radius and subsequent X-ray binary behavior. Based on existing data on transient neutron star X-ray binaries, along with their non-transient counterparts, a new statistical test has been developed to identify the proportion of quiescent systems that exhibit transient behavior. Utilizing this test and current observational data, it is estimated that roughly 30% of the Galactic Centre's quiescent neutron star X-ray binaries with low X-ray luminosities have sufficient accretion history to support transient behavior. This is consistent with the power that accretion processes have over the spin of the neutron star. Furthermore, it has been found that the transient recurrence interval of these systems is significantly influenced by their orbital period. A negative correlation has been observed between the two factors. Additionally, the findings suggest that the majority of the Galactic Centre's quiescent neutron star X-ray binaries with low Luminosities have recurrence intervals exceeding a few years, which has implications for future monitoring campaigns.

The abundance of wide binary stars in the Milky Way offers a promising approach to studying the effects of gravitational forces. However, the vast array of external influences on these stars complicates the problem, making it difficult to extract reliable information about their behavior under the influence of the galaxy's gravitational field. The theoretical model includes multiple factors such as the galactic disk, the galactic halo, the Large Magellanic Cloud, the Small Magellanic Cloud, the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, and the Sagittarius tidal stream. The model demonstrates how the presence of these external factors affects the distribution of wide binary stars and suggests that future observational data may be used to test the validity of these astrophysical influences or alternative theories of gravity through constraints on the galaxy's structure and composition.

We analyzed radio sources in three deep radio fields using sub-millijansky radio sources to stack around optically bright quasars at the same redshifts. Our study examines how properties of radio sources, such as power and orientation-averaged shape, are linked to their angular dimensions. To accomplish this, we created separate radio source stacks based on the cross-correlation of source position with major axis size at z=0.7. Our findings show that radio sources with larger angular dimensions tend to have more powerful radio emission, consistent with the picture that core-dominated sources are detected in variability-induced searches. However, we also discovered that sources with larger angular dimensions are more easily detected in searches for steep-spectrum sources, a phenomenon that could be caused by the bias in source selection. Our analysis specifically looked at sources with powerful radio emission, narrowing the selection to radio sources that likely exhibit high levels of jet energy. When considering the relationship between jet energy and sources with large angular dimensions, we found a stronger correlation between radio power and orientation-averaged shape, a property that could be linked to the beam's configuration, such that sources with large angular dimensions tend to have more collimated jets.

We analyze three-dimensional numerical simulations of massive stellar mass loss events driven by wave trains generated by multiple solar flares. These wave trains produce significant pressure and heat the surrounding atmosphere, potentially explaining the observed fast moving shock waves in coronae around massive stars following a supernova explosion. Our simulations show that the generated shock waves have temperatures of around 10 to 30 eV, explaining observed phenomena such as the high energy emission of supernovae like SN 1006, and that they may also create early blastwaves with energies comparable to those of supernovae, challenging the traditional single explosion mechanism for creating fast moving shock waves in the Milky Way. These simulations also indicate that wave trains can create shocks that travel at multiple speeds, potentially explaining observed variations in high energy emission of corona around massive stars following a supernova explosion, and that they may also create nasal wave structures, such as nasal spiral waves, and wave trains may also create shocks that travel at multiple speeds, and that they could also create wave trains that have never been observed before.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-abelian Calabi--Yau varieties to abelian ones. 
Specifically, it demonstrates that certain non-abelian, geometric objects of 
weight four are modular, building upon Diamond--Sasaki's work which addresses 
weight three objects. This involves applying a combination of geometric and 
algebraic techniques, including the use of Kuga--Sato varieties and Shimura 
variety geometry.

R. N. Berman (2021) proposed a self-consistent method for calculating the electronic properties of solids in relation to phonons and spin waves. This approach was successfully applied to derive a variety of well-known semiconductor equations. By extending Berman's method, we have developed a dynamic model that considers the interconnection between electrons and phonons (or spin waves), our model results in a deviation of the Kohn-Sham equations by the addition of a phonon (spin wave) field that is self-consistent in both time and momentum. Using this extended model, we derived the dynamic electron-phonon/spin-phonon interaction Hamiltonian in relation to momentum, a consequence of which is the phonon (spin wave) field having a significant impact on the choice of gauge that leaves physical results unchanged. Up to now, choices of gauge have been arbitrary, however this freedom allows for the optimization of gauge such that the phonon (spin wave) field's direct impact on the electron's behavior can be studied. This extension of Berman's method provides a connection between the charge and spin aspects of matter, establishing that spin waves can give rise to the scattering of photons by electrons, in accordance with the data provided by experiments carried out to date, as well as creating the possibility of photon-induced spin transfer, a phenomenon not observed in the conventional theory of electronics.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes aim to provide an accessible overview of the fundamental principles and some advanced aspects of $\tau$-tilting theory. We will explore the key concepts, including $\tau$-tilting modules and classes, as well as related notions like $\tau$-tilting dimension and the $\tau$-tilting graph. In addition, we will delve into specific topics such as the relationship between $\tau$-tilting theory and classical tilting theory, the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras with a focus on the Ext-algebra and its properties, and the connection between $\tau$-tilting theory and local calabi-yau categories.

Recent advances in Natural Language Inference tasks have been driven by AI models that rely on similarities and differences between sentences to grasp language. These advancements have sparked interest in applying Natural Language Inference to improve Dialogue Systems. To explore this potential, the study introduces a new challenge called Semantic Variety in Dialogue, which aims to investigate whether NLI models can capture the implicit meanings underlying dialogue scripts. In this context, Semantic Variety in Dialogue is redefined as a NLI task that determines whether a sentence is a relevant continuation of a dialogue. To assess the challenges facing NLI models in dialogue settings, the research introduces an additional sub-task called Reasoning Variety in Dialogue, which gauges the ability of NLI models to recognize the implicit reasons for a sentence in a dialogue. The study conducts experiments with NLI models on both tasks, using a newly created dataset called SemViD, and finds that state-of-the-art NLI models struggle to generalize to dialogue settings. To address this limitation, the research introduces a new model that successfully achieves the best results on SemViD, outperforming the previous best score by a significant margin of 11.8%. The study demonstrates that NLI models equipped with the proposed architecture can accurately recognize the implicit reasons for a sentence in a dialogue, achieving a score of 34.9% on the Reasoning Variety in Dialogue test set. The data and models used in this research are publicly available and can be accessed via the SemViD dataset repository.

Automated driving systems depend on robust multi-camera setups to ensure safety and effective navigation. However, developing reliable algorithms for their rearview cameras is a significant challenge due to limited visibility of rear hazards, particularly in critical maneuvers like changing lanes. This paper presents a novel approach to enhance the detection of hazards during such maneuvers by utilizing feature extraction from both the rearview camera and surrounding areas extracted by Mask-RCNN, along with RNN-based pattern recognition from the front camera. This method was tested on a specially created dataset called LaneChange (LC) and produced outstanding results, with a high AP score of 38.16% far exceeding the performance of existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

The occurrence of wind-induced angular momentum loss in low-mass stars and brown dwarfs is well supported by evidence, significantly influencing their rotational states and evolution. To better understand this process, we developed a numerical simulation modeling the rotation-driven convection of low-mass objects, incorporating both conservative and expansive scenarios, and validated the method against existing observations of main-sequence stars and brown dwarfs. By applying this simulation to various masses up to 15 Jupiter masses, we observed that wind angular momentum loss is necessary to explain the rotational characteristics observed in objects above 0.25 $M_\odot$. For objects below 0.25 $M_\odot$, the relationship between rotation period and convection zone depth breaks down due to the maximum rotation rates dictated by break-up velocity, and wind angular momentum loss becomes less influential as the rate of loss is outpaced by the internal generation of angular momentum.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in determining the amplitude coefficients 
due to the limited available data, especially when dealing with decay processes that 
involve more than two distinct final states. This issue is compounded by the fact 
that experimental measurements are subject to several influences that can impact their 
validity, such as different resolution functions, signal acceptance variations, and 
background suppression factors that vary based on the amplitude components. 
Consequently, the uncertainty associated with amplitude coefficients is significantly 
influenced by the experimental factors mentioned above, making it crucial to account 
for these effects properly to ensure the accuracy of physical interpretations. 
This talk will focus on the experimental factors mentioned above and their impact on the 
uncertainty associated with amplitude analysis, utilizing an actual example from 
heavy flavor research.

A new general model is proposed that dynamically tracks the afterglow phases of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) using radiative hydrodynamics and relativistic radiative transfer. Based on observations, a specific radiation component is identified that dominates the observed electromagnetic spectrum during the afterglow transition from radiative to adiabatic phases. Using this model, the distribution of GRB luminosities and their relationships with other physical properties are investigated to better understand the progenitor objects and physical processes that power GRBs. The model suggests that GRBs with long durations have larger Eiso values and lower density environments compared to those with shorter durations. A linear correlation between the energy released in the explosion (Eiso) and the amount of energy emitted in the afterglow (Safter), as well as a non-linear relationship between Eiso and the radiated energy in the prompt gamma-ray emission (Sp), are confirmed. The model also reveals that the density of the surrounding medium (n) varies between 10^-4 pc^-3 and 10^-1 pc^-3, with an average value of 8.5 x 10^-3 pc^-3. The model's predictions for the distribution of radiation energy in the prompt gamma-ray emission, the variability time-scale, the observed peak energy of the prompt emission, the total energy released in the explosion, the density of the surrounding medium, the true viewing angles, the radiated energy in the afterglow, the radiated

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their analysis often involves identifying the largest homogeneous subgroup within the graph. This study explores an efficient method for determining whether a given graph allows a specific subgraph configuration, based on the connection between its nodes. A key aspect of this approach is the ability to break down complex subgraphs into simpler components, represented by connected sequences of edges, and assign distinct labels to the nodes at their endpoints. This technique enables the reduction of initially intractable problems to manageable ones. A significant breakthrough in this area is the discovery of a algorithm that, for any given graph and subgraph, determines whether the subgraph can be replicated within the graph, using a method that breaks down the graph's edges into connected sequences, does so in a time proportional to the number of sequences, regardless of the overall size of the graph. Another breakthrough is the development of a method that, for any given graph and subgraph, determines whether the subgraph can be replicated within the graph, using a different method that breaks down the graph's edges into connected sequences, does so in a time proportional to the number of sequences, regardless of the overall size of the graph, and includes a condition that the connected sequences, when combined, form a cycle, although the order in which the nodes are visited is not fixed. Deep neural network classifiers have excelled in various tasks but may struggle with incremental learning due to their tendency to forget previous information. The problem is further complicated by the challenge of learning new classes without access to data from previous ones. Recent research aims to address this issue by proposing algorithms that can learn new classes while preserving knowledge from previous ones. However, most incremental learning algorithms are designed with the assumption that the number of classes remains constant, which is not always the case in real-world applications. To tackle this issue, new algorithms that can add new classes have been proposed, but they often struggle with data imbalance issues that commonly arise in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, a new task called imbalanced class incremental learning (ICIL) has been introduced, focusing on developing methods that can learn from a data set with an ever-expanding number of classes and a persistent imbalance issue. Given the complexity of ICIL, a new evaluation protocol that assesses an algorithm's ability to learn from a data set with a constantly shifting number of classes and a persistent imbalance issue over multiple trials has been introduced. A comprehensive evaluation of existing ICIL algorithms against a backdrop of increasing data imbalance issues has been carried out, but surprisingly, no unified calibration method has been adopted in the literature, despite the fact that deep neural network classifiers are known to suffer from various calibration issues. This paper will present our approach to enhancing the stability and efficiency of bipedal robots in dynamic environments using a closed-loop control system with a pair of thrusters. By rapidly adjusting their water/air flow, these thrusters can provide superior traction compared to traditional rubber thrusters, which are prone to slipping. We have developed a state-dependent switching control method that leverages the unique characteristics of our thrusters to switch between two different control strategies based on their angular velocity. This innovative approach allows our bipedal robot to maintain stability and normal gait using the same control strategy in both smooth and rough terrain environments, which has been successfully demonstrated through thruster-supported bipedal locomotion trials. However, further optimization of our thrusters and the layout of our bipedal robot's legs is needed to enable it to navigate through very rough terrain.

We define a specific type of domain, which we call valued domains with a total residue map, and demonstrate that they are equivalent to Hahn domains with a total order. This equivalence is the basis for a detailed study which includes the identification of continuous domain morphisms and the determination of when domains of this type are integrally closed.

Recent AI models, characterized by massive neural network layers and substantial distributed computation, are generating enormous interest in accelerated inference tasks. Despite the potential for significant speedups using multiple CPUs, real-world applications are constrained by power consumption limitations. In response to this challenge, I introduce HyperDegrade, a novel technique that leverages multiple CPUs to perform computation in parallel while reducing operating frequencies. Through HyperDegrade, a single GPU node can support complex AI applications with minimal accuracy losses, achieving a 2x improvement in batch sizes and 5x increase in inference rates. Furthermore, HyperDegrade on a single GPU node enables 24x24 transformer decoder layers on a single GPU node, surpassing leading transformer decomposition techniques in efficiency.

While numerous explanations for the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon have been ruled out by experimental limits on the Higgs sector, we investigate whether a simple Higgs-portal model can still contribute to this discrepancy. To do this, we consider two cases: the minimal Higgs-portal model, which involves a minimal interaction between the Higgs boson and a scalar field, and a more general Higgs-portal model with multiple interactions. Using a combination of existing constraints and our own analyses, we have identified a previously unexplored region that could potentially contribute to the anomaly. This unexplored region is constrained by direct search limits, such as LHC searches for the Higgs-portal dark photon, as well as constraints from dark matter abundance and Higgs invisible decay searches. Within this unexplored region, we have found that the Higgs-portal model could contribute up to 90% of the observed anomaly, with the minimal model contributing up to 20% and the general model up to 90%. To better understand the possible connections between the Higgs sector and the muon g-2 anomaly, further experimental and theoretical studies are needed.

A calculation is presented of the CKM phase gamma from a combination of functional fits to three-dimensional decay branch distributions, utilizing 3.0 femtobarn of -7 and 7 TeV collision data from the CMS experiment at the LHC. This analysis is based on final states featuring one or two leptons and uses a range of event selection criteria and likelihood fit functions that incorporate resonance decays and two-body decay patterns. The resulting value of gamma is 0.606 pm 0.012, with a closure test confirming the robustness of the measurement.

We define a novel disentangling operation for closed braids, which we call the "double single braid operation." This action effectively unwinds specific closed braids by generating a sequence of closed braids composed of nested simple closed braids. We establish that a closed braid can be completely disentangled into a product of 2-crossing braid powers if and only if it can be transformed into a product of 2-crossing braid powers under the double single braid operation. This discovery leads to a determination of whether a closed braid can be fully disentangled into a product of 2-crossing braid powers. Additionally, we introduce a geometric method to find the closed braid obtained by applying the double single baid operation to a given closed braid. This method enables the identification of whether a closed braid can be fully disentangled into a product of 2-crossing braid powers. Furthermore, we extend the double single baid operation to closed welded braids and investigate its properties.

Let's consider a tropical curve that's connected, finite, and non-trivial. If we denote this curve as C, we can establish a rational function semifield denoted as k(C). Furthermore, if we define a finite set of generators for the tropical curve as V, we can express it as the disjoint union of finite, connected components. Based on this relationship, we can establish that the rational function semifield of the tropical curve, k(C), is finitely generated over the semifield of rational functions associated with a tropical line, k(A). This conclusion follows from analyzing the finite, connected components of the tropical curve and recognizing that the rational function semifield of the tropical curve is finitely generated over the semifield of rational functions associated with its components.

We've demonstrated that the Fox-Hatcher derivative of a long knot's 1-cocycle, specifically with respect to a specific set of generators, embodies a Vassiliev invariant of order three. Consequently, this integral invariant is inherently invariant under the action of braid groups. Furthermore, we have previously established that the space of 1-cocycles susceptible to this derivative action across a particular set of generators seamlessly aligns with the space of Vassiliev invariants of order two, thereby establishing a direct relationship between them. Building upon this finding, we now extend this connection to include the domain of 2-cocycles in relation to the Fox-Hatcher derivative, revealing that such derivatives result in precise combinations of order three Vassiliev invariants when considering the Chebarikov-Faddeev progression, a relationship that can be seen to stem from the underlying properties of the Chern-Weil theory.

New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are below 0.8 eV. In this study, we examine how this finding affects lower limits on the neutrino mass spectrum, specifically the minimum mass for the more heavily weighted sin^2(theta_1) component, which is currently set at 0.71 eV by OA bounds from the Super-Kamiokande data alone. Combining this with the KATRIN result, we find the minimum mass for the sin^2(theta_1) component to be 0.59 eV. Additionally, we found that the recently reported electron neutrino geo-electro-magnetic disintegration data by the KATRIN collaboration, presented as upper limits on the neutrino cross-section at 39 MeV, when combined with existing OA bounds from the Super-Kamiokande data, result in a minimum mass for the sin^2(theta_1) component of 0.66 eV, with the overall neutrino mass spectrum minimum at 0.69 eV.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, tasks are often divided into parallel components that require synchronization to complete. We refer to this concept as multi-task synchronization. Considering a system where the performance of individual agents is constrained by their processing capabilities and inter-agent connections are limited to a regular network, we investigate the achievable synchronization rates for a significant class of tasks. Specifically, we show that the maximum sustainable rate is directly proportional to the connectivity of the network and is unaffected by the specific structure of the tasks. Furthermore, we find that a regular network's connectivity is essential for achieving high synchronization rates with a large number of agents. To validate our theoretical findings, we compare them to actual performance in a series of simulation experiments.

In quantum field theory, infrared safety is a crucial property for physical observables, and their precise measurement requires the accurate elimination of large logarithmic diverences at small scales. Despite advances in combinatorial and symmetry-based approaches, achieving precise insights into infrared-safe observables remains challenging. The amplitude-based resummation, a proven strategy for tackling these complexities, has shown significant success in simplifying the interpretation of data in searches for new physics at the Large Hadron Collider. However, there are still issues to be addressed, such as the impact of infrared modes on sensitivity to new physics and the relevance of threshold effects. This talk will provide an update on the latest developments in amplitude-based resummation, addressing these open questions and highlighting the importance of consistently applying this approach across different theoretical and experimental studies.

This paper uncovers the difficulties in implementing secure multi-party computation (MPC) protocols in Federated Learning (FL), particularly when data cannot be coordinated. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, centered on private query protocols, in addressing these challenges. We show that certain popular FL use cases can lead to substantial leaks of sensitive information and present strategies to circumvent these issues. Moreover, we introduce an original concept, 'leakage-resistant FL,' aimed at private data analysis. The purpose of this work is to encourage researchers and practitioners to reevaluate the privacy guarantees embedded in FL systems. The accompanying supplementary material includes a detailed walkthrough of the protocols discussed in this paper along with additional theoretical proofs.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. To overcome this hurdle, Random Fourier Features were proposed, allowing kernel methods to utilize random projections and achieve comparable performance at a significantly lower computational cost. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring a fixed kernel function and an arbitrarily large amount of memory. To address these issues, this paper presents a novel kernel estimation technique based on data dependencies, which significantly reduces the computational cost and requires substantially less memory. Our experiments demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms the standard RFF approach in multiple benchmark scenarios.

We'll be investigating how a group is embedded into a wreath product using the Cartesian breakdown approach. This includes examining factors such as whether the embedding preserves group properties like normality or conjuugacy, and also exploring the relationship between the generators of the group and the wreath product.

This research paper examines how conformal mappings affect the concept of Mobius scalar curvature on compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces in Euclidean space with five dimensions or higher. Specifically, it investigates whether a duality-based approach can utilize conformal mappings to establish the existence of Mobius scalar curvature with specific properties on these hypersurfaces. The paper's main finding is that conformal mappings can indeed enable the existence of Mobius scalar curvature with specific properties on these hypersurfaces, provided that the hypersurfaces satisfy particular symmetry conditions. The paper also explores whether a similar result can be established for closed, conformally flat subsets of Euclidean space with four dimensions.

In congenital heart disease, pre-surgery planning is critical and accurate cardiac anatomy assessment is essential. Advanced imaging like magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides this assessment through automatic cardiac segmentation. Despite being widely used, our risk of death from congenital heart disease is declining, making rare forms of the disease even more infrequent. As a result, large datasets for training machine learning models, particularly those based on deep learning like U-Net, are scarce for automated cardiac segmentation. This study investigates the performance of a commonly adopted U-Net model, specifically for ventricle segmentation, when trained on a relatively small dataset of CMR images from adults with tetralogy of Fallot and used for segmenting heart defects due to left ventricular non-compaction. We discovered that while the model excels when applied to its own dataset, its efficiency and accuracy decline when applied to a new, similarly-structured dataset. This limitation is not unique to deep learning, as we also observed significant performance differences when applying a model trained on a dataset of normal hearts compared to one trained on hearts with tetralogy of Fallot. Notably, the model performed remarkably well on ventricle segmentation when used as a prior for fully automated segmentation of a new, unseen dataset with a relatively low error rate of 5.4%. This study has implications for selecting models and their applications in medical fields where data is scarce and anatomical understanding is key.

This research focuses on an extensive class of non-linear materials found in various applications, which are characterized by localized damage in the form of distinct cracks. To accurately model this type of damage, we utilize a novel approach that involves a specific degradation mechanism. This mechanism, which affects the material's stiffness, is represented by a specific function influenced by the crack's geometry and location. To model the material's response to external loading, we apply a computational method that utilizes a specific finite element technique. This method involves solving a system of non-linear equations through an iterative process, with the solution being the material's reaction to the loading. As the loading intensity increases, the material's reaction will eventually approach a point where the cracks' effect on stiffness is significantly impacted, resulting in the material's failure. This model can be used to study various aspects of the material's response to loading, such as how the size and location of the cracks influence its reaction, and can also be applied to solve practical problems involving this type of material.

A new paradigm in multi-service wireless communications is presented, based on a novel approach that combines the transmission of information with the harvesting of energy (SWIPT). An integrated system, capable of serving multiple users with different services, is considered. A key component of this system is a multi-antenna transmitter that forms tailored signals for various receivers, taking into account the possibility of SWIPT. To optimize performance, a method of transmitting information and energy is identified and a corresponding distribution strategy is proposed. Furthermore, a practical implementation is described, involving a mathematical problem that is solved using an optimized algorithm. The effectiveness of this approach is confirmed through the conduct of statistical analyses, yielding valuable insights that can be applied across various contexts. The resulting model offers a versatile solution that can be applied to a range of scenarios and variations.

Object detection in deep learning is often viewed as assigning confidence and a set of coordinates to potential bounding boxes. A common limitation of this approach is the focus solely on objectness, which can lead to missed detections when only a few bounding boxes are considered. This problem is compounded by the fact that encoding spatial information within the bounding box coordinate system can obscure the contribution of the confidence score. To address this limitation, transforming the detection problem into a two-stage process has been proposed. In the initial stage, the goal is to identify all possible objects across a predefined range of bounding box dimensions, rather than constraining the search to assumed object forms. This yields a more flexible and expansive set of potential bindings, which can then be pruned based on size in the subsequent stage. To improve efficiency, incorporating spatial intermediate supervision within the bounding box dimension hierarchy has been found to be beneficial. Through this reformed detection framework, substantial gains in Miss Rate at a 1% False Positive Rate are achieved on the COCO benchmark, outperforming the state-of-the-art by $8.0\%$ when evaluated on the VOC07 test set.

As structural models including those based on Graphical Models and Factorization Models have been widely using Conditional Models to infer causal relationships, a category of models that assumes independence conditioned on a set of variables, a critical characteristic of such models worth examining is the extremal trait. In a recent study, the extremal trait of structural models was found to correlate with the causal interpretability of the models. To investigate this further, the current paper aims to systematically explore extremal traits across diverse conditional models using a new metric that assesses extremal traits in graphical representations. The results indicate that certain conditionally independent distributions can be achieved by multiple families of structural models, highlighting the significance of considering the underlying distribution when inferring causal relationships from observational data. Moreover, the paper introduces the concept of causal over-specification to describe the phenomenon where models based on different causal structures produce the same predictions, which has implications for the use of model-averaging methods. The analysis of extremal traits across diverse conditional models can lead to a more comprehensive understanding of the causal interpretability of structural models.

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to tackle this problem, we must first recognize the issue's scope, which is compounded by the lack of standard evaluation metrics for WSD in over 70 years of research. 

To address this challenge, we draw from WSD competitions that utilize the LAMBEC and LWOAC datasets, which feature sentences with annotated target words whose meanings are deduced through contextual analysis. Our approach builds upon the strong BERT-based baseline model introduced by Huang et al. and involves a multi-step process to tackle the task at hand. 

1.  **Contextual Inference**: We begin by training a model to predict the target word's meaning from its surrounding context. To improve the baseline model's performance, we explored various enhancements, including the incorporation of word embeddings and the use of BERT variants, and found that the addition of character-level embeddings yielded the most significant gains.

2.  **Target Word Embedding**: To effectively identify the target word within the sentence, we experiment with both sentence- and target-word-specific embedding techniques, ultimately finding that the latter yields the best results.

3.  **Sentence Re-ranking**: We investigated the integration of learning-based and non-learning based sentence re-ranking methods to refine the model's performance.

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events are crucial components of sophisticated reasoning ability, closely tied to real-world applications such as planning and narrative understanding. Despite being fundamental skills, sequencing remains an unexplored area of research in the context of multimodal procedural knowledge. In contrast to the extensive work on natural language inference, a survey of popular datasets revealed that none comprehensively assess the sequential structure of ordered events in a single dataset. Consequently, we introduce the Multimodal Storyline Sequencing (MSS) dataset, comprising two variants (MSS-Con and MSS-Inf) that examine the ability to sequence events based on both procedural and inferential relationships in visual narrative guidebooks. Formally, the task involves classifying ordered event pairs as correctly or incorrectly aligned. Our preliminary experiments using a simple vision-and-language model revealed promising performance, with results indicating a gap in performance between the Con and Inf branches. Furthermore, an analysis of the data and obtained results shed light on the challenges posed by sequences that do not follow a linear structure. We believe that the MSS dataset will serve as a valuable resource for exploring the intersection of sequential reasoning and the analysis of ordered events in a multimodal setting.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating robust networks and understanding the underlying dynamics of complex systems. Researchers often study network susceptibility by analyzing critical phenomena, such as percolation and epidemic spreading, which can induce failures or fluctuations in network performance. In this study, we investigate another indicator of network vulnerability, the distribution of avalanche magnitudes in response to random node removals. Our analysis is conducted on Cayley trees of varying degrees, and the results show that the distribution of avalanche magnitudes follows a power law that transitions between two distinct exponents corresponding to the network's local and global components. The findings are validated through numerical simulations and theoretical modeling, and the distribution is shown to be influenced by the degree of node attachment, with higher attachment degrees resulting in larger avalanche magnitudes. This research provides insights into the avalanche-magnitude distribution of networks and offers a framework for studying dynamic processes in networks.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are severely limited by energy loss mechanisms at high signal frequencies. Two major sources of this loss are laser phase noise and signal-recording thermal noise in the photodetector. To combat this, researchers are exploring novel detection schemes that minimize signal amplification and move the photodetector signal demodulation process closer to the carrier, thereby reducing thermal noise. Two possible approaches, the heterodyne and homodyne detectors, have been analyzed, with the former demonstrating improved sensitivity at high frequencies but compromised DC sensitivity, and the latter exhibiting improved DC sensitivity but reduced high-frequency sensitivity in certain configurations. With further advancements in signal-recording technologies, the detectors may surpass the projection-based sensitivity at frequencies above 200 Hz.

Recent research in massive MIMO has led to significant advances in understanding the visibility region and its implications. A novel random access protocol called the XL-MIMO protocol was developed to capitalize on non-intersecting visibility regions in a multi-user setting. This protocol enables a high level of spatial reuse and minimizes collision probability. However, the protocol's limitations arise when there are a small number of users with fully overlapping visibility regions. In such cases, alternative protocols like the LM-MIMO protocol may perform better. Nevertheless, various scenarios have been identified where the XL-MIMO protocol excels, including those with a large number of users with partially overlapping visibility regions, low signal-to-noise ratios, and fading that obstruct line-of-sight transmission. Furthermore, the optimal density of base station antennas within this context has been found to be directly proportional to the square root of the number of users.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter and millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, such as rings and spirals. Prior research suggested that these patterns originate from the gravitational influence of mutually orbiting objects within the disk. However, the findings of this study indicate that certain exotic structures, such as spirals opening at more than 30 degrees, ring gaps opening in more than 60 degrees, and spiral patterns separated by more than 1.5 times the hole at their innermost point, cannot be explained by the gravitational effects of embedded objects. These specific features may be caused by density fluctuations caused by the Shear Instability in vertical layers of the disk. Models incorporating the reflection of light from the disk's surface and dust particles predict the spectral energy distribution and spatial distribution of dust in various environments surrounding young stars. Using these models, we analyzed observations of AA Tau, MHD-driven shear instability models, and models of vertical shear instability for a range of parameters. The results show that the sensitivity of the observation of the vertical shear instability model depends on the sensitivity of the dust continuum observation in the spatial distribution and spectral distribution. If the separation between the two objects in the disk is less than 430 AU, the observation of the vertical shear instability model will not confirm the presence of the instability. If the separation is greater than 130 AU, model confirmation is likely. The most critical factor in confirming the model is the spatial resolution, with

The 'Big Apple' strength, a measure of the harmonic strength of the shell model, is examined in a comprehensive way. Initially, calculations for the ground states of major nuclei using the mass tunneling method are performed to derive the Apple strength. Further analysis is then conducted for individual harmonic components across the nuclear chart. In addition, the relationship between the Apple strength and other shell model properties such as magnetic moments and decay widths is explored. Specifically, calculations are undertaken for decay widths of low-lying states in odd-$A$ isotopes via the operator product method. The connection between the Apple strength and macroscopic properties like density and its distribution around the nucleon cluster in the center of mass frame is also investigated. The results show that the Apple strength displays a clear correlation with the density of nuclei. In conjunction with the Lorentz distribution, a simple formula for estimating Apple strengths based on density is derived. The study demonstrates that the harmonic strength of the shell model, reflected in the Big Apple strength, exhibits a clear relationship with the density of nuclear matter, a concept that could be applicable across various phases of nuclear matter including neutron star matter.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the complexities of 3d transition metal physics within this compound. A detailed analysis of the lattice model derived from first principles reveals a mixed-valence state in SrMnO$_3$, characterized by intermediate coupling between the d electrons and the lattice. To overcome computational limitations, we developed a method to efficiently solve the impurity problem using the Dynamical Mean-Field Theory Solver, tailored for large systems when only real frequencies are available. This breakthrough enables researchers to explore the physics within a broader class of materials that were previously inaccessible, and our study showcases its utility within the context of SrMnO$_3$.

Our analysis reveals a method to create resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates under steady-state laser illumination. When operating with long-lived species like calcium ions, this technique becomes particularly crucial due to ion-detection limitations which prohibit the application of classical phase-contrast techniques. By incorporating multiple balanced motional modes into the Gaussian light pulse used in Gaussian optics, this method achieves Molmer-Sorensen gate durability without hindering efficient and accurate ion detection via laser-induced fluorescence. Monte Carlo simulations simulate this process for (174)Yb+ and (40)Ca+ ions to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

Using machine learning to generate structures and ab initio calculations, we've found a new method to predict the spontaneous polarization in paraelectric perovskites by identifying and modifying certain features in the crystal lattice. Specifically, we've determined the specific arrangements of atoms and bonds that contribute to polarization, and demonstrated that simply recognizing these patterns is enough to make accurate predictions about polarization without needing detailed computational simulations of the physical properties. This breakthrough enables the rapid assessment of polarizability in new materials with unprecedented accuracy, potentially paving the way for breakthroughs in technology.

We utilize a razor-thin layer of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ to experimentally observe a strongly correlated Dirac metal. By comparing our findings to existing theoretical predictions for this system, we gather substantial evidence to support the presence of a Kondo-Cooper ladder phase near the Dirac points. Additionally, we successfully demonstrate that a Kondo-Cooper ladder phase can be achieved without the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling by utilizing a strong interaction that respects rotational symmetry. Furthermore, we show that the hallmarks of this phase, including the long-range interaction and strong correlation with the Dirac electrons, can be engineered by selecting an appropriate substrate. The predicted theoretical results indicate that the system will exhibit a strong correlation with the Dirac electrons, and the onset of this correlation will be marked by the deviation from the linear T dependence of the total gap, as well as the failure to fit Mott's law due to the Mott-Insulator phase that the system will eventually enter at very low temperatures.

We present a novel statistical framework that tackles identical problems – testing the null hypothesis of a binary distribution's proportion equality across categories and testing the null hypothesis of a bimodal distribution's component proportion equality across categories. This framework is versatile, as it can handle both categorical and continuous data with user-defined thresholds, and it provides a comprehensive approach to bimodal testing by first testing unimodality. We investigate the asymptotic behavior of our test statistic and establish a theoretical distribution under which it relies on a chi-squared test. We also assess the test's performance through numerical simulations of varying sample sizes and bimodality depths. The results show that the test's accuracy is sensitive to sample size, with the test performing up to 25% better when doubling the sample size. The method is implemented in an R package named 'bproptest'.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles.
