This paper presents a novel data-driven biophysical model of Parkinson's disease, drawing from electrical patterns observed in the brains of marmoset monkeys. Our model was created using a high-performance computing platform and is characterized by more than 10,000 interacting biological components. To verify the model's accuracy, a range of parkinsonian symptoms similar to those in human patients have been successfully recreated. Furthermore, the model showcases significant potential for optimizing treatment methods through computational techniques and real-world animal studies.

The proliferation of mobile devices and online map platforms necessitates optimized visualizations of large-scale maps for improved user experience. Specifically, the rendering of line joins in map graphics poses a performance challenge, particularly when incorporating spatial anti-aliasing for a more polished appearance. In this research, we revise the conventional multi-pass technique for spatial anti-aliasing involving line joins, replacing it with a single-pass algorithm that leverages the capabilities of programmable graphics processors. The new method yields significant performance gains while delivering a high-quality, anti-aliased visual effect. To validate the proposed technique, a comparative analysis of the original and revised algorithms is conducted in the context of a commercial map application. The findings indicate that the revised method achieves a 2.5-fold increase in frame rates on high-end mobile devices, paving the way for the widespread adoption of spatial anti-aliasing in line joins across various map platforms.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of the galaxies, (2) stronger at later stages of merger, and (3) linked to the temperature of the gas. Our observations suggest a relationship between the gas outflow, the temperature of the gas, and the power source of the galaxies, and highlight the importance of optical IFU spectroscopy in the study of galaxy merger.

The multivariate interpolation operator is often used to approximate functions in multiple variables. In this study, a new interpolation operator is developed, leveraging a recently proposed transcendental RBF, to efficiently and accurately approximate functions worldwide, preserving their non-negativity and providing an approximation that oscillates a set number of times as its input does.

Cloud types serve as a crucial element in understanding atmospheric phenomena, 
which are vital in studying astronomical phenomena such as the formation of planetary 
systems and the early stages of star formation. Clouds also play a critical role in 
regulating planetary temperatures. Researchers have traditionally employed linear 
techniques to classify clouds based on their angular appearances, but these methods 
have limitations when dealing with complex and dynamic phenomena like cloud formations.
The introduction of non-linear methods such as neural networks has made it possible 
to model the relationships between cloud features and their classifications more effectively.
However, applying these models to cloud data is complicated due to the high cost of 
acquiring labeled training data, the need to address issues of overfitting, and the 
limited availability of datasets.
The WCR dataset presented here addresses these concerns, comprising over 10,000 high-quality 
images of weather conditions from around the world and providing a comprehensive 
benchmark for evaluating the performance of neural networks in real-world scenarios.
To further improve model accuracy, a novel data augmentation technique is also 
introduced, combining local low-frequency transformation with local frequency 
separation, resulting in the achievement of an outstanding model that surpasses human 
classification error rate.

Deep learning-based audio enhancement has seen significant advancements in recent years with the introduction of low-latency and high-performance methods. A dual-path convolution recurrent network is introduced in this paper to further improve single-channel audio enhancement. This novel framework effectively handles non-stationary background noise and overlapping speech by utilizing dual convolution recurrent modules with distinct data paths. Experiments conducted on the ICASSP 2020 evaluation dataset revealed that the proposed DPCRN model surpasses state-of-the-art techniques like DCA-DNN and MIMOSA, demonstrating its potential in real-world applications.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to assess the interaction between $f(R)$ gravity and sterile neutrinos. Using the MICECAT catalog with 1257 cluster halos, this methodology reveals a 2.5$\sigma$ deviation in favor of the $f(R)$ gravity model when neutrinos are massless. Additionally, the data indicates a radii shift of $\sim 0.36c$ due to the effects of massive neutrinos. The most probable cross-section for the turn-around radii change, related to the $f(R)$ gravity model, is estimated at $\Delta\chi^2=12.4$ for a confidence level of 95.4%, with a corresponding value of $\sigma=0.54$ and a range of possible values for $M_\nu$ between 0.06eV and 1.60eV. The results highlight the distinct signature of $f(R)$ gravity on the distribution of matter at high scales, with a difference in the parametric space compared to cosmological simulations. The introduced methodology offers a new approach to investigating the relationship between $f(R)$ gravity and massive neutrinos using observational data.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A similar technique, the single-fluid model, achieves similar results but with a more conventional approach, nonetheless requiring the same level of fine tuning. Nonetheless, the ultimate goal is to develop an optimal control strategy for feedback control using model-based control methods. Despite the potential benefits, the current state of atmospheric modelling is not conducive to implementing such a sophisticated control system due to the absence of a fundamental physical model. In atmospheric applications, the primary driver of convection is temperature differences within small layers of ascending and descending air, resembling the dynamics observed in Rayleigh-Benard convection. This paper presents a basic two-fluid representation of this phenomenon, incorporating a similar physical model that accurately replicates the associated heat transfer. The model incorporates a perspective interface and fluid flux operator, both amenable to numerical solution using a similar discrete formulation to that of the multi-fluid model. The associated numerical scheme is discussed, along with a rudimentary verification of the model using a simple single-column simulation.

We investigate three separate cases of entangling dichotomic two-level atoms that are not connected and do not share quantum states. In the first scenario, we show that a specific combination of Jaynes-Cummings interactions with a single coherent light beam is sufficient to create an arbitrary dichotomic entanglement between the atoms. Additionally, we find that using a parametric family of unitary transformations achieves this goal. Furthermore, we find that the same outcome can be achieved with minimal light-atom coupling strength and in the long-time limit of steady-state conditions. In the second scenario, we find that the same outcome can be achieved through the action of a single classical light field when the atoms have distinct resonant frequencies. In the third scenario, we find that the same outcome can be achieved when the atoms share classical classical vacuum states and have the capacity for two-way classical communication.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. Within this detector, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. During the LHC's initial operational period, a pilot module featuring an 8x25 mm^2 silicon pixel pilot blade (RPX) prototype was integrated into the forward pixel detector. Despite being located near the beam line, this prototype successfully contributed to the reconstruction of particles' paths. Through detailed analysis of data obtained before the switch to the full detector, the pilot module's performance was assessed, with results indicating the prototype's effectiveness in identifying particle events, tracking trajectories, and calculating physical properties such as momentum.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral distribution function of the SU(2) glueball, utilizing the elastic scalar form factor obtained from lattice QCD with the configuration of $N_f=2$ $N_c=3$ and a lattice spacing of $0.04$, based on data from Ref.[1] with an imaginary time interval of $\Delta\tau=0.1$. This approach involves the transformation of the spectral distribution function into the spectral density distribution function, which can be directly computed from the elastic scalar form factor via the spectral representation. This computation yields the spectral density distribution function for four different values of the momentum $p$. Notably, the magnitude of the spectral density distribution function at the origin is found to be in the order of $10^{-3}$ GeV$^5$, in line with the findings from Ref.[2].

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based model was developed to predict the sentiment expressed in the data. The model
was trained and its performance was evaluated using the annotated data. Several evaluation
metrics were used to compare the proposed model's performance to that of existing sentiment
analysis models.

A new non-linear theory for gravity within Anti-de Sitter spaces is used to create a charged black hole with a non-spherical shape caused by a specific type of matter. Researchers have studied how this matter affects the temperature of the black hole's surface, known as the "Hartle-Hawking boundary", when it is subjected to light from a distant source. The temperature of the boundary was found to depend on the angle of the light and was calculated for a specific type of non-spherical black hole. The relationship between the temperature of the boundary and the electromagnetic charge of the black hole was also examined in various situations. The temperature of the boundary can be affected by the presence of a specific type of matter, leading to a change in the electromagnetic charge of the black hole over time. The rate of this change is determined by the temperature of the boundary. The temperature of the boundary can also be used to determine the rate of energy loss from the black hole due to light emitted from the "Hartle-Hawking boundary". The temperature of this boundary is not the same as the temperature of the black hole's surface in other areas. The temperature of the boundary in these other areas is influenced by the presence of a specific type of matter and is not directly linked to the electromagnetic charge of the black hole. The temperature of these areas can affect the rate of energy loss from the black hole due to light emitted from these areas. The rate of this energy loss is found to be linked to

The tomographic representation of quantum states offers a comprehensive understanding of both their classical and non-classical characteristics. Through tomographic Wigner functions, we can further analyze the entanglement properties of states and the effects of environmental interactions. Utilizing the Lynge-Heinonen-Maniscalchi approach, we can derive specific quantities that indicate the level of entanglement, based on the Lloyd's susceptibility decay rate. This rate is notably influenced by the environment's coupling strength and system size. Specifically, our findings show that in multi-mode Gaussian states, there is a distinct threshold below which entanglement is minimal, and that this threshold is unrelated to the system's size. Furthermore, we observed that the onset of synchronization among system components is intimately connected with the decay of Lloyd's susceptibility and the entanglement properties of the system.

Building conversational interfaces for various settings, like customer service or personal assistants, requires a significant amount of work. Creating such systems involves developing multiple dialogue systems with varying characteristics, such as tone, level of formality, and expertise. Typically, these systems are designed to cater to specific domains or topics, but there's also a need for systems that can engage in open-domain conversations. Typically, these systems are designed to engage in open-domain conversations. Typically, these systems are designed to engage in open-domain conversations. Currently, large language models excel at generating human-like text, but they struggle to adhere to roles and specifications during open-domain conversations. Therefore, there's a need to investigate new methods for integrating these models into role-specified dialogue systems. One potential approach involves training a single dialogue model to cater to various settings, but another approach is to combine multiple smaller models, leading to improved performance on specific tasks. In this paper, we explore the latter approach, combining the strengths of large language models with smaller specialized models, to develop a single dialogue system that can handle multiple roles. This combined model delivers superior performance on role-specified dialogue tasks when compared to a state-of-the-art large language model, according to human evaluators. Additionally, we find that this approach is particularly effective at preventing the degradation of performance in open-domain conversations.

Effective pest management strategies are crucial for maintaining a healthy and productive crop yield. To evaluate the efficacy of these management strategies, researchers use statistical methods to assess treatment impacts and estimate confidence levels. Unfortunately, the accuracy of these estimates can be compromised when data non-compliance becomes a issue. In the case of field experiments with pests, data non-compliance often results in the presence of outliers, which can skew estimates and render them unreliable. Furthermore, the inherent spatial correlations present in these data fields another challenge for researchers to overcome. To address these limitations, we developed a robust method that utilizes the quantile regression approach in combination with spatial analysis. Specifically, we employed the Dunn-Shawver method to account for spatial correlations and the influence function to counter the effects of outliers. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we applied it to a dataset related to the management of strawberry diseases. The results showed that the method's estimates were more accurate and less prone to bias than traditional approaches. The method's advantages are particularly beneficial for researchers tasked with evaluating pest management strategies that involve complex treatment designs and exhibit significant spatial correlations.

360-degree virtual tourism videos provide immersive experiences for viewers, but the vast amount of information presented can be overwhelming and may lead to perspective-taking difficulties. To facilitate more effective engagement and exploration, this study proposes a perspective-prediction model based on subtitles embedded in the video. The model leverages data from search engines and combines with a 360-degree video analysis framework to suggest viewers where the creator of the video is looking. Experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves notable advancements in accuracy when compared to a control group.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling many-body systems, 2D systems at thermal equilibrium, and systems undergoing time evolution. However, these algorithms generally involve approximations that compromise the accuracy of these representations, particularly the trade-off between entanglement density and computational efficiency. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel tensor network algorithm based on locally optimized approximations, enabling the accurate depiction of entanglement dynamics while maintaining computational tractability. This method involves locally refining the tensor network ansatz through the correction of tensor shapes, a protocol that is efficiently achieved via the application of thermal perturbation tensor networks. Our proposal is a concrete realization of the idea of entanglement purification, a concept initially conceived theoretically. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have numerically simulated various scenarios, including the simulation of thermal states, entanglement dynamics, and quantum quenches, using the FTGSQSD algorithm, which yields satisfactory results.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in positive characteristic. Our approach involves expressing a surface as the result of applying a set of linear transformations to a standard form. We then employ a combination of Taylor series expansions and approximations to define a local structure near the origin, ultimately establishing a decoupling inequality for functions within this local structure. This framework enables us to generalize previous decoupling results from previous papers, particularly those by the second author and Li for smooth surfaces, and by the first author and the second author for quasi-smooth surfaces, to a broader class of surfaces, including those with non-smooth points, in both characteristic zero and positive.

This study examines how the Minkowski inequality is affected by anisotropic $p$-capacitance in the Euclidean space. We initially prove that this inequality remains valid when the anisotropic $p$-capacitance is associated with a symmetric matrix with nonnegative eigenvalues, which includes the case of self-adjoint capacities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the anisotropic $p$-capacitance is linked to the Sobolev inequality, which in turn enables us to establish a broader inequality that connects the anisotropic $p$-capacitance to the anisotropic Minkowski inequality. We then investigate the conditions under which the anisotropic Minkowski inequality holds true for any set of finite measure.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. These masses experience non-gravitational forces due to the motion around our planet, algebraically summed as $Q_{\rm tot} = Q_{\rm drag} + Q_{\rm radiation} + Q_{\rm grav}$. Gravitational effects originate from tidal interactions with the Earth and its oblateness. To accurately determine the WEPS violation, it's crucial to assess how statistical and systematic uncertainties impact the measurement. The former is dominated by the drag force, which is linked to the drag coefficient and the mass ratio between the test masses and their surrounding environment. The measurement of the WEPS violation is also affected by glitches, or sudden changes, in the signal that result from the interaction of the test masses with the spacecraft. These events, which are relatively rare, typically last seconds to minutes. The glitches investigated in this study exhibit a diverse range of characteristics, including distinct signatures, correlated motions, and abrupt variations. The most influential glitches on the measurement of the WEPS violation need to be identified in order to assess the test's validity. The variety of glitches observed during the mission pose a significant threat to the accuracy of the test, with some glitches potentially affecting the measurement by as much as 10 times the predicted limit.

We investigate the behavior of colloidal molecules in activity gradients created by swimming particles that are bound together. Our findings show that the rotation of these colloidal molecules around their axis can vary dynamically, depending on the activity gradient. In certain situations, the angle between bound particles may fluctuate, allowing the system to transition between different shapes, ultimately influencing how the system interacts with surface obstacles. This complex dynamics is influenced by several factors, including the activity gradient, the strength of the binding between particles, and the size of the particles. Through our research, we gather extensive data on these fluctuations, validating our theoretical predictions with multiple experiments that mimic different conditions.

The k-SSPC problem requires finding the minimum number of shortest paths in a graph G that, when combined, satisfy all pairwise source-destination connections, given that each path has a maximum capacity of k. In this study, we examine the k-SSPC problem in certain graph types, specifically undirected trees, directed acyclic graphs, and multi-commodity flows with integer capacities. We present a method for computing the k-SSPC collection using a union of k shortest paths, as well as a way to determine whether a k-SSPC collection exists for these graph types.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution function is examined, and it's found that they significantly influence the behavior of gluon distribution at small x. As a result, the infrared renormalon ambiguity in the TMD PDF is observed to increase with decreasing x, indicating a $x^2$ growth in the TMD PDF at very small x. Furthermore, within the scope of impact factor formalism, the infrared renormalon ambiguity in the TMD PDF is found to be dominated by the impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole GDFF, specifically for semi-hadronic processes like p+A->A+H.

As the number of frogs per site exceeds two in the frog model on a binary tree, percolation occurs. This statement holds without the requirement of transitivity. The necessary condition for percolation, depending on the frog density, is determined in terms of the degree of the tree.

Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create ultra-fast, multi-functional optical devices. One approach involves combining rare earth ions with localized energy and transition metals that adjust magnetization, to achieve extraordinary optical phenomena under magnetic fields. Yet, current methods do not allow for the precise alignment of these materials at the surface, light propagation depth, or magnetic field orientation. This study introduces an unconventional technique of strain-induced arrangement, utilizing elastomer templates replicated into photonic surfaces. It demonstrates the capability to design structures that display distinct magnetic field-dependent phenomena, such as changes in reflectance and polarization. By manipulating the strain, it is possible to achieve unprecedented levels of composition and structural complexity. This method offers a versatile means of manufacturing complex magnetic, optical, and multifunctional materials at the surface, enabling precise control over magnetophotonic properties.

As artificial intelligence systems become ubiquitous in everyday life, ensuring their reliability and user safety is increasingly critical. In order to comply with regulations such as Section 15 of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, it's essential to implement measures like expunging knowledge from predictive models that process sensitive information. However, the lack of accessible training data and algorithms for neural networks complicates this task. This paper introduces a novel approach that enables the removal of knowledge from complex neural network-based classifiers by utilizing decision-based black-box models, without requiring access to the underlying architecture or training data. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in transferring knowledge from modified source models to target environments without retraining, a process known as zero-shot knowledge transfer. This innovative technique has the potential to streamline the safe deployment of AI systems in various settings.

Researchers have observed two hitherto unseen rare phenomena in physics using a dataset of 3.0 inverse femtobarns of data collected from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Specifically, they have detected the occurrence of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ processes. To better understand these events, physicists employed various methods to confirm or reject the expected theoretical branching ratios, ultimately finding the observed rates of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ to be $2.8\pm0.4$ and $2.0\pm0.3$ times larger than predicted by theory, respectively. Furthermore, this discovery has significant implications for studying other $b$ hadron decays into $c K$ final states with negligible background from primary $b$ quark production.

Given a module $M$ and a subset $\Pi$ of submodules of $M$, the lattice of submodules of $M$ denoted as $\con(\Pi)$, consists of all submodules of $M$ that can be obtained by closing the set $\Pi$ under meet and join operations. In this study, conditions are established under which $\con(\Pi)$ is finite or reachable based on the relationship between elements of $\Pi$. Additionally, the problem of finding the maximum clique in a poset is recognized as an instance of determining the conditions under which $\con(\Pi)$ is a lattice, and the term "poset lattice reachability problem" is proposed to describe this broader challenge.

The geodetic set problem in graph theory is solved in polynomial time by utilizing a binary matrix representation, but when confronted with uncertain or incorrect vertex connection data, the problem becomes significantly more complex. This paper investigates the robust geodetic set problem by analyzing its computational intractability and the limitations it imposes on reducing other $\mathsf{NP}$-complete problems. This includes a proof that certain variants of the binary matrix representation do not aid in solving NP-complete problems efficiently. This research also compares the robust geodetic set problem to other graph theory problems involving uncertain connections between vertices.

The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal examples. Nonetheless, obtaining a large number of high-quality examples is frequently hindered by significant expenses. In this paper, we address this issue by analyzing what it means to have a sufficient number of examples for imitation learning and providing a criterion that indicates how many examples are required in a given MDP setting. We also developed a trial-and-error algorithm called TRAIL that determines an optimal subset of nearly optimal examples for imitation learning from the available data. TRAIL's performance was evaluated in various gridworld environments, and the results showed substantial improvements over current state-of-the-art methods like DeepMind's Rewinding, Multi-step Rewinding, and several baseline algorithms.

To accelerate the learning pace of reinforcement learning agents in complex tasks, imitation learning from expert demonstrations has been effectively combined with their training. However, the limitation of this approach lies in the expense and difficulty of obtaining a substantial number of high-quality demonstrations, especially in scenarios where expert data is scarce. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel learning algorithm called Counterfactual Imitation Learning (COT), which bypasses the need for expert demonstrations altogether. COT trains agents to explore counterfactual policies - i.e., policies observed through the lens of inverse reinforcement learning - in parallel with the target policy. The agent then learns to prioritize the visitation distribution of the counterfactual policy when updating the target policy, either explicitly or implicitly. As a result, the agent can learn efficient behavior without expert guidance, outperforming the baseline agent trained via vanilla reinforcement learning in various scenarios.

This paper calculates the performance metric, known as the pivot or cutoff rate, for a specific type of code called the partial-erasure code (PAC code) and provides comparisons with other codes that correct channel noise, specifically the maximum-likelihood decoder (MLD) and the binary erasure channel (BEC) code. Furthermore, this paper showcases the superiority of PAC codes over MLD codes in scenarios where specific types of channel noise are present.

Using reinforcement learning in neural machine translation has been a subject of interest in recent years. One notable issue with RL models is their excessive number of possible actions, which hinders the effectiveness of policy-based models. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel search space reduction method called the Packed Vocabulary Search (PVS) model, which significantly expands the range of possible actions while maintaining computational efficiency. In experiments, our PVS model achieved superior performance to Packed Neural Machine Translation and Monte Carlo reinforcement learning models on WMT en-de and en-fr translation tasks.

In this research, a novel approach is presented to enable a robot to estimate its pose and end-effector position in relation to a static depth camera, without the use of markers, in a scenario where the surrounding environment changes. This methodology leverages machine learning, specifically Deep Virtual Map (DVM), a framework developed in our lab, to create and utilize a dataset that facilitates efficient development and deployment of DVM-enabled systems. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through experiments using a simulation and real-world data, showing improvements in accuracy over traditional SLAM methods in scenarios with moderate to fast environmental changes.

In this study, we establish a new framework called quasi-Fock space (QFS) that incorporates a set of polynomials resembling the Fock space polynomials. Within this framework, we identify a specific region called the QFS-region and prove that it satisfies a key property: the QFS-space can be expressed as an overlap of QFS-regions multiplied by a specific set of polynomials. Additionally, we show that the QFS-region is invariant under a specific group called the U_q(su(2)_+ group.

The disparity in online news consumption habits between liberals and conservatives cannot be fully captured by existing studies. To address this limitation, this paper compares left-leaning and right-leaning online news consumers in their browsing habits, social connections, and political alignment. Our investigation involves 25 participants who identified as either liberal or conservative and completed a series of tasks on a custom-built website. The results showed that liberal users and conservative users exhibited distinct browsing behaviors when visiting news websites, with liberal users displaying greater curiosity and a preference for exploring new topics, and conservative users preferring a more familiar news feed with minimal risk of exposure to opposing views. In contrast, when given the option to hide friends with opposing political views, both liberal and conservative participants chose to display such friends. Notably, four conservative participants in our study opted to hide friends with the same political views, suggesting that online social connections may not always align with an individual's political ideology. Additionally, our findings indicated that online users' political beliefs may not always reflect their offline beliefs, potentially leading to the diffusion of misinformation through social connections.

We'll examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a complex generating function, specifically one that generates a sequence whose terms are composed of an exponentially growing subsequence and another subsequence whose growth is governed by a polynomial of very high degree. This polynomial degree is currently unknown, but it is known that any potential proof of the word problem being soluble would necessitate the existence of a fraction whose denominator has a growth rate that surpasses an extremely high polynomial. Any potential proof of the word problem being insoluble would require the existence of a fraction whose numerator or underlying group properties exhibit growth that surpasses a very high polynomial. We'll also investigate whether this word problem belongs to a particular class known as the context-free languages, and discuss the implications of this investigation in relation to the group V itself.

To understand the steady-state behavior of microscopic systems subject to periodic fluctuations, it is necessary to analyze their response in a situation far from thermal equilibrium. This study investigates the steady-state regime of a superconducting quantum bit driven periodically by microwave radiation, with the aim of establishing a link between its observational data and Liouville's equation that simulates the system's behavior over time. By comparing observations with calculations, we can determine the non-equilibrium fluctuations of the system in its steady state and how they are affected by different parameters. Furthermore, we can use these results to interpret measurements obtained from actual experiments.

We explore how various mechanisms affect biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space. By establishing connections between the Laplacian and Jacobi operators, we identify key characteristics for biharmonic hypersurfaces under specific operational conditions. Notably, we determine that certain actions on harmonic and minimal hypersurfaces lead to non-existence, while specific actions on periodic hypersurfaces suggest the possibility of existence. Additionally, we establish relationships between the recurrent mechanism and other conditions, demonstrating that certain operations on recurrent hypersurfaces result in periodic hypersurfaces.

A continuous function on an interval can be accurately determined by a finite number of relative positions of intervals containing its values, relative to its minimum and maximum. This concept is often referred to as p/q-identifiability. The paper explores the conditions under which a subset of a continuous function corresponds to a p/q-identifiable set. It is shown that if a subset of a continuous function is p/q-identifiable, it must be an interval. The paper also investigates the conditions under which an interval of a continuous function is p/q-identifiable. It is shown that if the interval is finite, it is p/q-identifiable if and only if the function is monotonic within that interval. The paper further investigates the conditions for an infinite interval of a continuous function to be p/q-identifiable, and provides a necessary and sufficient condition in terms of the asymptotic behavior of the function's minimum and maximum. The paper also presents an example of an interval of a continuous function that is p/q-identifiable but not monotonic within that interval, and the identifiability of intervals of continuous functions on the real line.

We investigate how the addition of sterile neutrinos and a fundamental axion field affects gravitational collapse. Considering a right-handed neutrino sector that induces algebras within the Fock space of sterile neutrinos, we find that their wave functions correlate with each other. This, in turn, leads to the formation of a non-local, long-range interaction between sterile neutrinos. As a result, we predict that matter made up of axion-sterile neutrino (aNeu) matter fields will interact with each other in a similar manner to conventional matter during gravitational collapse. This aNeu matter may provide an explanation for the phenomena associated with dark matter.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a series of observations for a time-domain survey on four K2 plates. These observations, amounting to over 1800 exposures in 632 blue spectra, were obtained across 3868 unique targets. By utilizing the LAMOST's own radial velocity standard stars and calibrating the zero-point, the team was able to determine the radial velocities for their targets. These results demonstrate the capability of the LAMOST to conduct high-priority astronomical research, including radial velocity cross-correlation, and showcase its potential as an astrophysical tool for studying variable objects.

In image analysis, particularly with medical images, semantic partitioning is an advanced technique that automates object definition and boundary estimation. However, this process is challenging due to high-dimensional data, noise, and variability in patient anatomy. Current methods primarily utilize encoder-based architectures, combining CNNs with transformer models, but these tend to focus on surface detection rather than volumetric analysis. To address this limitation, this study proposes an edge-gated convolutional neural network, integrating a gated mechanism to direct feature flow and a global context network to capture global anatomy. This unique architecture is applied to MR images for the automated segmentation of organs and tumors. Experimental results on the MICCAI 2016 challenge dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

MongoDB is a widely used NoSQL document-oriented database that employs a transactional storage engine called Mongose. Mongose is based on the Storage Manager for Document Engine (SMDE), a transactional storage engine that maintains document isolation. SMDE ensures isolation through a coherence mechanism called coherence zones. To guarantee that coherence zones operate correctly, a formal specification known as the coherence protocol is used. However, the large and complex nature of the SMDE code makes verifying the coherence protocol manually prone to errors. To address this challenge, we developed a store specification that provides a clear and concise overview of the SMDE storage system. Using this store specification, we created a formal specification of the coherence protocol using separation logic and verified its correctness using the F* verification framework. The results of our verification revealed several key findings, including the proof of correctness for the coherence zones protocol, as well as modifications to the SMDE code that ensure transactional coherence.

We establish the positivity of specific coefficients in the chromatic symmetric function basis, relative to the monomial basis, for all combinatorial classes whose underlying set has a cardinality of three, based on the properties of the inverse Kostka matrix. Furthermore, this analysis enables us to devise an algorithm for computing the chromatic symmetric function of any combinatorial class whose underlying set has a cardinality not exceeding three. Additionally, we make use of the same theoretical framework to demonstrate the $e$-positivity of the Popovici-Shapeerafter the Stanley-Drake conjecture.

We begin by defining a task where agents both observe and experience the consequences of actions within an environment. We demonstrate how a single perceived outcome affects multiple locations and offer a method to condense this outcome into a summarized perception. We aim to enhance the conditional probability of a specific action being performed, given a particular perception of the environment. To achieve this, we filter out irrelevant experiences, readjust the significance of environment components, and refine the perception of the environment using a strategy that contrasts desired outcomes. We showcase the effectiveness of this strategy in various scenarios, including the manipulation of complex internal states and the selection of optimal paths.

The accuracy of medical image diagnosis models depends on various factors, including the characteristics of the data used to train them. Unfortunately, the field of medical image analysis lacks effective tools for assessing data bias. In order to create a reliable framework for identifying and quantifying bias in medical image data, we first define key terminology and concepts related to data bias. Then, we propose a systematic approach to evaluate data representativeness, applying this to popular datasets in the field. Our findings reveal concerning levels of bias in datasets used for training and testing segmentation models. To mitigate these issues, we believe it is essential to incorporate statistical analysis into the construction of high-quality medical image datasets, incorporating representations of various demographic groups.

We introduce a novel strategy to uncover the underlying geometry and dynamics of intricate networks by using a topological reduction method. This approach involves simplifying complex graphs into their most fundamental components, thereby identifying the essential structural elements and revealing the underlying dynamics. As a demonstration of this technique's effectiveness, we examine nanoassemblies consisting of triangles and isolated nodes, and show that our method accurately identifies the critical parameters that lead to magnetic reversal. Furthermore, we find that the proposed strategy is highly efficient, with minimal computational requirements, even for large-scale networks.

Between 0.025 and 0.17 AU from the Sun, the flow of plasma in the solar breeze is controlled by solar gravity and a pressure gradient driven by solar wind pressure. This range includes the vicinity of the Sun's Alfven radius, thought to influence the orbital path of solar particles around coronae. The speed of the plasma breeze was measured during close approaches to the Sun by the Parker Solar Probe and was found to be between 595 and 1044 km/s. The pressure of the plasma breeze was calculated and compared to model predictions, showing that energy flux varied greatly, impacted by temperature and density. The results also indicated that the energy flux of the plasma breeze is a significant component of solar wind energy flux, especially in the inner heliosphere near the Sun's Alfven radius. The data from the UARS and three solar instruments on board the Parker Solar Probe were used for this analysis.

Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. However, the disparity between trained models and real-world data affects their practical application. This research aims to bridge this gap by adapting deep reinforcement learning to modify the training data, enabling the accurate detection of speech emotions in real-world scenarios.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of hydrostatic pressure on its magnetic properties.  Unpolarized He$^3$ nuclear forward scattering was utilized to analyze the dynamical and static magnetic correlations  within BFTO at various pressures up to 12.5 GPa.  Our findings reveal that BFTO exhibits ferrimagnetic behavior at ambient pressure, aligned with prior research.  Upon increasing pressure, the magnitude of the magnetic moment remains relatively constant, whereas its orientation changes, and there's evidence of magnetic stiffness enhancement with increased pressure.  Interestingly, a first-order magnetic transition was discovered at 8 GPa, resulting in antiferromagnetic order, a phenomenon not predicted in lattice models commonly employed for this family of compounds.  This new phase is characterized by unique spin correlation, and we propose the existence of a pressure-induced phase diagram for BFTO.

Discrete-shortest path algorithms are commonly used to solve complex planning problems, including free flight optimization, by breaking down the continuous problem into manageable discrete components. However, relying on approximations here may introduce significant errors, especially when the discrete representation deviates significantly from the actual continuous space. In contrast, an alternative approach based on continuous shortest path algorithms can minimize errors by maintaining a detailed representation of the continuous space. However, this approach often requires more significant computational resources. A comparative study between these two methods, specifically using the A* algorithm for discrete shortest paths and the dynamic programming algorithm for continuous shortest paths, sheds light on the trade-offs between error and computation in the context of free flight optimization, with implications extending to other similar planning problems.

Researchers have discovered that the distribution of galaxy clusters follows a specific, dynamic pattern linked to the cosmic shockwave. This shockwave's location is tied to the virial radius of clusters and affects the cluster's formation and growth. Studies have revealed that the shockwave's intensity decreases as the universe expands, limiting the growth of clusters. A new study has investigated how the cluster's formation is affected by the presence of a spherical void within it. Scientists found that the void's existence doesn't significantly impact the cluster's overall structure but does affect the distribution of matter within it. Due to its location at the edge of the cluster, the void's impact is mainly felt by the cluster's outermost particles, which have the highest relative velocities. This effect could be observable in cluster observations, particularly in clusters surrounded by large voids similar in size to the Coma cluster. Scientists also discovered that the void's presence slows down the cluster's net velocity as it moves through the cosmic web. As a result, the cluster takes longer to cross a given distance, an effect that could be linked to the phenomenon of cluster acceleration observed in the web.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the differential decay rate for the process $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is found to be in the form $R(q^2) = \frac{d\Gamma}{dq^2} = \frac{d\Gamma^{\mathrm{MC}}}{dq^2}\left(\frac{R(q^2)}{R(0.25\mathrm{GeV}^2)}\right)$, with $R(q^2)$ displaying significant variation across the measured range of $0.05$ GeV$^2$ to $1.30$ GeV$^2$. Furthermore, through the use of NRQCD by the lattice QCD collaboration for the quark level process $\bar{d}b\rightarrow \bar{c}s\gamma$, a theoretical prediction for the rate has been made, resulting in a χ^2 value of 16 for 25 degrees of freedom, giving a p-value of $0.996$.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorifying the properties of specialized polynomials, specifically the generalized Hermite polynomials. These advances enable a better comprehension of monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential. The paper's authors explain the relationships between these polynomials and the associated Schrödinger operators, providing a review of previous research and the recent breakthroughs in the field. The authors also explore the link between the polynomials and the Weyl-Heisenberg algebra, examining the role of the algebra in the construction of the Schrödinger operators. The paper concludes with a discussion on the potential for further research in the area, considering the involvement of Fock spaces and the algebra in deriving results about the Schrödinger operators' spectra.

A persistent issue in studying non-uniform noise patterns is the lack of a clear framework that can capture the underlying dynamics. Our research involves an experimental setup where adhesive tape is peeled apart while the noise it produces is recorded. Unlike previous work, our approach deviates from conventional methods in two key ways. Firstly, we're not solely focused on measuring the time between occurrences - instead, our analysis centers on the relationship between the spacing of events and the time it takes for them to happen. Secondly, our method involves an unconventional comparison where the ratio of event spacing to time between events is constant, which facilitates direct integration. This comparative approach allows us to bypass the need for differential equations. Our findings consist of a database of diverse noise patterns, each characterized by a unique constant ratio. This constant ratio governs the dynamics of the noise pattern, offering a clear picture of the underlying dynamics for the first time. Our research suggests that the noise generated by the peeling of an adhesive tape contains a wide range of noise patterns, evolving continuously through a predictable trajectory.

In this project, we studied the behavior of superconducting circuits containing long, narrow Josephson junctions and performed precise measurements of the magnetic interference pattern. Our findings revealed unexpected shifts in phase at very low magnetic field strengths, which increase exponentially with the decrease in temperature. This phenomenon becomes most pronounced at extremely low temperatures near the critical point of superconductivity, where the phase transitions become very slow. We investigated the influence of different types of noise on this behavior and found that certain noise sources cause the system to switch between different states, while others divert the current around the SQUID loop. Our research also showed that the phase shifts vary depending on the type of metal used in the SQUID and the length of the Josephson junction. We were able to measure the minimum energy required for a magnetic flux quantum to traverse the circuit and observed that it is determined by the resistance of the normal state and is in line with theoretical predictions that the energy is proportional to the square of the resistance.

The Yang-Mills ether action is re-examined with a non-abelian extension of the standard Euler-Heisenberg action. By converting the Yang-Mills field into a non-abelian Maxwell field using a non-abelian duality transformation, the Euler-Heisenberg action is re-expressed in a non-abelian extended Maxwell-Dirac model. This transformation allows for a similar analysis in a hot QCD plasma utilizing the Hard Thermal Loop (HTL) dynamics. With this approach, the non-abelian extended Euler-Heisenberg action can be computed in a hot QCD plasma using the HTL Lagrangian for massless quarks and gluons within the one-loop approximation.

This research develops an advanced mathematical method for determining the minimum amount of money required to sell a specific type of option, taking into account both the option's potential gains and losses and the costs associated with executing underlying asset trades as part of a dynamic delta hedging strategy. Specifically, the approach is applicable to options with discrete price movements and a specific renewal process, and involves computing expectations based on the underlying asset's joint price changes with its delta. A specific example is explored where the underlying asset follows a geometric Brownian motion process, and an alternative method of determining the margin is also examined. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how the cost of delta hedging can be estimated using the volatility of the underlying asset's returns and the delta of the option, and highlights the robustness of the results to changes in the duration of the option.

This research focuses on the long-term behavior of a variety of mixtures with disparate properties, characterized by partial differential equations (PDEs) with significant contrasts in their coefficients. The project extends the capabilities of existing methods by relaxing a key symmetry condition, while also exploring alternative techniques for handling a specific constraint that reflects the mixture's physical limitations. Through the study of a specific PDE with contrasting coefficients, the research reveals that the underlying process can be described by a simplified model that represents the average mixture behavior.

This study focuses on identifying early-type galaxies with large tidal features that are detectable in images taken more than two years after their initial observation. Using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program, we discovered 1,076 such galaxies at a significance of more than 3.5 sigma. These findings were further validated through mock galaxy simulations. We found that tidal features in these galaxies account for 0.15% to 0.25% of their total light, and their features are typically shorter than 30 kiloparsecs. In a follow-up analysis, we examined the ratio of tidal features to galaxy size, and this ratio varied significantly, ranging from 0.1 to 0.5, with no apparent correlation with galaxy brightness. We also investigated the rate at which these galaxies merge with others, and this rate was found to be quite high, likely exceeding 10% per billion years, which is more than twice the rate estimated for spiral galaxies. This discrepancy may be attributed to the fact that early-type galaxies are more massive than spiral galaxies, and thus tidal features in early-type galaxies contribute a more significant proportion of their mass.

A social mobility cycle with an unlimited number of generations distributes endogenous opportunities among descendants based on the actions of their ancestors. The mechanism determines the opportunities allotted to each family and the incentives it provides to individuals within that family. The mechanism's efficiency is optimal when the discount rate is zero, and it achieves this by multiplying the discount rate of the social mobility cycle by a constant greater than one. This causes the discount rate of the cycle to be less than the rate implied by the discount factors of the individuals within it. As a result, the distribution of opportunities assigned to each family is greater than the implied rate, which in turn allows the mechanism to sustain itself without any external support.

In the realm of optics and photonics, system design plays a leading role in creating innovative technologies. While the underlying science is well understood, the intricate details of system design seem elusive, making it difficult to assess the technological advancements in this field. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by providing in-depth analysis of cutting-edge laser systems, highlighting their design, strengths, and areas for improvement. Specifically, we examine amplitude and phase control in femtosecond laser development, spectral broadening in supercontinuum generation, and nonlinear fiber dynamics. By applying this knowledge, we outline strategies to enhance fiber laser systems, identify potential applications for supercontinuum-based spectroscopy, and successfully replicate a diode-pumped mean-power record-breaking fiber laser. Our work is expected to inspire the next generation of photonics researchers, providing a thorough understanding of the complex relationships between science, technology, and engineering in this field.

Moreover, when $p>2$, we prove that for any given $\epsilon\in (0,1)$ and structured set $K\subseteq \ell_p$, there exists a linear transformation $T:\ell_p\to \ell_p$ such that $\|T\|=\epsilon\cdot \|Id\|_{\ell_p\to \ell_p}$ and $\|T^{-1}\|=\epsilon^{-1}\cdot \|Id\|_{\ell_p\to \ell_p}$, with an intrinsic property that $T$ shrinks the dimension of $\ell_p^K$ by an arbitrarily large fraction, i.e., $\dim_{\

To effectively monitor beam dynamics, a rapid screening method called brightness scanning is implemented at the ADJOI scanner located at the HHI user area of the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR). This scanner, utilizing a flat panel detector and a moving slit, measures transverse beam distributions and performs a variety of diagnostic tasks. As a result of upgrades to the scanner's power supply and data acquisition system, it is now possible to conduct brightness scans at higher beam currents and with greater precision. Consequently, a new diagnostic tool has become available for monitoring beam dynamics and performing emittance measurements.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a deviation from the optimal solution when cooperative methods are employed. To address this issue, a distributed subgradient optimization algorithm based on quantization and robustness is developed to minimize the negative impact of malicious behavior. The solution obtained through this algorithm approximates the optimal solution at a rate proportional to $1/\sqrt{k}$, where $k$ denotes the number of iterations. Additionally, the paper investigates the trade-off between communication constraints, represented by quantization, and the robustness against malicious behavior. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is tested on a supply chain management problem, which demonstrates its effectiveness.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental approach in cosmology, and experiments like CMB saveers are at the forefront of this research. To accurately interpret data from these experiments, it's crucial to simulate their instrumental characteristics. However, the vast parameters spaces associated with $n_s$ and $E(Bess)/\ell$ make this task challenging. To address this issue, we've developed a stochastic model of instrumental effects on microwave background experiments, and this model is part of the cmb experiments toolkit known as s4cmb. This model simulates cross-polarization biases, net polarization efficiencies, and beam shapes to provide realistic simulations of data from such experiments. To validate this model, we compared its output with that of a comprehensive end-to-end simulation pipeline used for the Cosmo-WebT project, and we found it to be a reliable and efficient tool for analyzing the impact of instrumental biases on microwave background experiments.

In the context of language generation, the task of arranging words to form a coherent sentence has not been extensively explored, although it seems inherently connected to the task of text generation. This study delves into the capabilities of a pre-trained language model, specifically BART, in word arrangement tasks, involving both simple sentences and sentences requiring the use of a relative clause. Our findings indicate that BART's performance in these tasks is comparable to its performance in standard language tasks, and it achieves these results through a unique set of syntactic dependencies that are often localized around specific words. This knowledge was utilized to investigate the extent to which BART's capacity to recognize and replicate syntactic patterns from a large corpus of text enables it to produce complex sentences with specific structures. Our analysis offers a deeper understanding of the relationship between the syntactic structure of language and the distribution of symbols, providing a foundation for exploring the interplay between syntax and semantics in language models. This research is a initial step in a broader investigation aimed at clarifying the extent to which the structural aspects of language influence the semantics, and whether the intricate nature of language can be a source of its own complexity.

The emergence of deepfake technology poses a significant threat to both individuals and society as a whole. Deepfakes can be highly convincing video forgeries that are increasingly difficult to detect. To combat this emerging danger, a robust detection framework is urgently needed. In this paper, our primary objective is to showcase a versatile detection approach known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which is designed to identify deepfakes in various video formats across multiple domains. This approach leverages a cross-stitching unit to combine feature extracts from two distinct neural networks, enabling the recognition of deepfakes in diverse video domains. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed MD-CSDNetwork achieves superior performance compared to existing detection methods, as evidenced by outstanding results on the Celeb-DF and DFD datasets. Furthermore, we introduce an extension to the Celeb-DF dataset known as the Celeb-DF-V2, a more comprehensive and versatile dataset that accommodates real-world video forgeries in multiple domains. Our code and extended dataset are available for download at https://github.com/ghiboskhadi/md-csdnet.

Current research examines the performance of binary low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes when transmitted over a binary deletion channel with random code ensembles. Studies have shown that under certain conditions, well-designed LDPC codes can achieve very close results to the maximum possible rate for reliable transmission. However, little is known about the effectiveness of LDPC codes when they contain degree-degree correlations. To bridge this knowledge gap, a novel random LDPC ensemble was recently proposed that allows degree-degree correlations. To facilitate the transmission of LDPC codes over the binary deletion channel with high data rates, researchers propose a new method for constructing LDPC codes with degree-degree correlations. This method enables the creation of LDPC codes with a wide range of degree distributions, including those that do not satisfy the standard Gallager bounds. Consequently, better error-correction performance can be achieved for high-rate LDPC code transmissions over the binary deletion channel.

Our investigation into the decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD system reveals a critical vulnerability. An adversary can launch a real-photon-gaining source hacking attack which involves two distinct strategies. Depending on whether the system employs random phase bases or partial phase randomization, the attacker can employ two respective approaches. We discovered that the positive outcomes resulting from measuring the basis corresponding to the phase randomization of the source are significantly reduced when the system utilizes partial phase randomization. Consequently, the attacker can generate real-photon gains which could compromise the system when the degree of phase randomization is low. Nonetheless, we found that implementing a random phase base system can be vulnerable to hacking. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose a novel approach that involves incorporating a measure that indicates the degree of phase randomization in the system. This enables users to select the most secure system based on its physical characteristics. Our findings underscore the significance of thoroughly examining the source of the system to forestall hacking attacks.

As 5G networks are being deployed, the increasing number of devices and users are straining the infrastructure, leading to concerns about the long-term sustainability and self-organizing capabilities of these networks. To address this issue, this paper presents a novel approach that focuses on decentralized management, enabling 5G networks to autonomously detect and resolve issues with core network infrastructure. Leveraging the OpenAPI framework, our system allows for the creation of application programming interfaces (APIs) that facilitate the secure and trusted exchange of information between network entities. Furthermore, our approach incorporates penalty-based methods for optimizing network resources and a decentralized approach to managing core network functions. To evaluate the effectiveness of our system, we conducted simulations under realistic scenarios, observing a significant reduction in core network administration costs (ranging from 20% to 60%) and notable improvements in response times (up to 90%).

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in a non-Euclidean geometry that utilized angle spaces, which are now referred to as Menger spaces. However, Menger acknowledged the presence of an underlying issue within his theory, which concerned the consistency of certain statements regarding the relative angles between certain lines. This led him to pose two problems to the mathematical community, which remained unsolved for over sixty years. In this study, we present a method that not only resolves these problems but also showcases the uniqueness of the solutions within the context of Menger spaces. Additionally, our findings can be applied to generate new examples of non-Euclidean geometry within three-dimensional space, which meets specific distance requirements, which was first achieved by J. Rosenberg using a different method.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in a total field $M$ of degree $d \geq 2$, and an order $\mathcal{O}_0$ in $K$. We present a non-trivial inequality relating the successive minima of $\mathcal{O}_0$ in $M$ to the coefficients of a binary form defining an embedding of $K$ into $M$. Furthermore, we establish that this inequality cannot be improved in general, and it enables us to derive a previously known result by Chaudury and Kumar, as well as a novel result regarding the invariant of a curve associated with an order in a number field.

We utilize a 1-d fs/ps hybrid technique in rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS) with dual probes to detect multiple gas parameters from oxygen, nitrogen, and nitrogen-dioxide with a 10 pm spectral resolution. By combining probes at two distinct frequencies (-0.15 g/cm^2 and 0.05 g/cm^2), we can determine pressure, temperature, and O2/N2 mole fractions accurately. The method offers precise detections of pressure (0.5 bar), temperature (1 K), and O2/N2 ratios (0.1), enabling the analysis of turbulent flows, complex combustion processes, and biological observations of respiratory systems with high spatial integrity. The technique's efficiency is further enhanced by enabling dual-probe detection with a single laser system and no moving parts, facilitating the exploration of previously unmeasurable phenomena.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets and the structure of protoplanetary disks are used for comparison with the simulated results, showing that this process can significantly impact disk evolution and the formation of planetary systems.

In the context of tumor tissues, research suggests that electric fields can play a crucial role in angiogenesis, a process which is vital for tumor growth. This paper presents a mathematical model to analyze the effect of electric fields on angiogenesis, powered by alternative current sources representing the 0.1 Hz bioelectric currents detected in humans. We demonstrate that the proposed model yields a specific current that is comparable to the observed bioelectric currents, thereby validating the model's realism. Furthermore, we show that the model allows for the distribution of the 0.1 Hz current across various pathways, enabling a better comprehension of its functional aspects. Building upon this model, we introduce a new approach to electric field generation, utilizing direct current sources to replicate the electric field patterns observed in tissues. This new method demonstrates a strong correlation between the dc electric field and its components, providing a more integrated view of the bioelectric phenomenon.

We introduce a cluster character $\mathcal{X}_\mathcal{A}$ for a set of algebra generators $\mathcal{A}$ within the quantum group $\mathbb{U}$, associated with the symplectic Levi subgroup $\mathrm{Sp}_{2r}(\mathbb{C})$ of rank $r$. This character $\mathcal{X}_\mathcal{A}$, depending on mutable variables $x_\mathcal{A}$, is a composition of the original character $\chi_\mathcal{A}$ by a transformation that is invariant under Mautner's twist. The value of $\mathcal{X}_\math{A}(1)$ is expressible as a ratio of two variables from the cluster algebra $\mathcal{X}$, specifically variables central to the Lusztig's quiver, and this value is connectable to a central extension of the Weyl group algebra through Morita equivalence. Moreover, $\mathcal{X}_\mathcal{A}$ is integrable to a refined character $\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}_\mathcal{A}$, which is a $\mathbb{Z}$-linear combination of refined extremal weight characters of irreducible $\mathbb{U}$-modules. The coefficients of these characters are identifiable with a specific basis of the central algebra $\mathbb{Z}[\mathfrak{S}_n]$, and these characters exhibit a connection

In machine learning, reducing overfitting through data regularization is a common practice, particularly when working with limited and diverse data. A similar concept, centered around reducing bias in the data, is relatively unexplored. This study introduces an equilibrium-based decentralized learning framework that addresses bias in the data by formulating a proper scoring rule, thereby connecting the framework with a significant body of research. We then leverage the beta-Bernoulli distribution as an example of a non-degenerate distribution to illustrate the framework's applicability. Furthermore, we investigate the theoretical properties of the proposed framework, focusing particularly on its connection to the total variation distance and the ability to achieve optimal bias regularization through decentralized optimization. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework through numerical experiments conducted on various datasets.

In the late 1980s, computer simulations experienced an explosive growth 
following a significant reduction in costs associated with storage capacity, 
which in turn enabled researchers to generate comprehensive datasets consisting 
of numerous time series. This advancement paved the way for researchers to 
devote a portion of their computer time and storage capacity to intricate tasks 
and allowed them to conduct detailed investigations of complex processes on a 
larger scale. One such process is the sediment transport network, which 
involves considering numerous variables, non-linear interactions, and diverse 
timescales. To tackle this challenge, researchers introduced a variety of 
non-traditional methods that drew from various disciplines, including physics, 
biology, and economics, and drew inspiration from the Hard Drive Project, 
which aimed to model the behavior of rivers globally. This historical review 
explores the evolution of hard-drive simulations, from their inception to the 
present day, and highlights the lessons learned, the remaining challenges, 
and the potential for further advancements in modeling dynamic systems on a 
global scale.

This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with jet production at a scale, nuclear parton distribution functions, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and elliptic flow data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results, with a specific focus on medium-modified jet production within a 0.35 GeV caustic region. Additionally, differences between PYTHIA 6.4 and JEWEL simulate distinct primary and fragmentary jet components, respectively. Various parameters including nuclear parton distribution functions, medium temperature, and shear viscosity-to-entropy ratio are investigated to understand their impact on interpreting medium-modified jet production data from the LHC.

The cryptocurrency industry has seen significant growth in the past decade, 
shaping the way people invest, earn, and interact with each other. Despite 
these positive developments, the rise of cryptocurrency has created opportunities 
for scammers and con artists to operate and profit. One relatively recent 
type of cybercrime involves sophisticated pyramid schemes and fake investment 
projects built on blockchain smart contracts. These systems leverage referral 
based compensation, empty promises of high returns, and complex and opaque 
contract code to deceive and swindle victims. The Forsage scheme, the subject 
of this study, is a notable example of this kind of crime. Forsage is a decentralized 
matrix program that promises affiliates substantial returns on investment, 
claiming to be an e-commerce platform that pays affiliates for promoting 
digital products. However, an examination of the project's code, combined 
with data collected from within the system, reveals a comprehensive and detailed 
picture of this scam, including the massive sums of money involved, the 
extensive network of participants, and the geographical reach of the scheme.

Our team investigated 19 potential globular clusters located in the bulge of the Milky Way, utilizing infrared images from the VVV survey. We utilized three different methods to determine the distances to these potential clusters, which yielded results that were relatively consistent. Subsequent analysis of their stellar populations using the AGB and RR Lyrae stars in the clusters did not match the expected characteristics of a globular cluster with a low metal content, suggesting they might be more similar to an old open cluster. Additionally, the concentration levels of the clusters were found to be lower than that of typical globular clusters, further indicating this distinction.

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders, specifically for the LHC and future facilities like the HL-LHC and FCC hh, rely heavily on accurate predictions for color-singlet differential distributions in hadron production. Given the significance of these predictions, it is crucial to incorporate the leading and subleading terms in various expansions, including the small-aperture approximation, the small-virtuality approximation, and the small-mass approximation, to ensure the desired level of precision. This paper focuses on the small-virtuality approximation and presents a comprehensive overview of the impacts of massive quarks on the DY process, emphasizing the role of $m_Q^2/L^2$ in governing these effects, where $L$ is a logarithmic distance. It highlights the challenges in incorporating these effects at the differential level and presents a viable approach for combining them with other corrections via coherent NLO corrections within the Soft Collinear Effective Theory. This allows for the resummation of large logarithmic distances and suppressed mass effects, facilitating the derivation of precise quark-mass dependent and logarithmic corrections and their implementation in numerical code using the Matchbox library. This provides a clear path for integrating the effects of massive quarks into matching prescriptions that account for massless and massive NLO dynamics in the data-driven approach and enables the construction of precise exclusive distributions at the LHC and future hadron colliders.

We utilized a tight-binding model that accounts for all atoms to systematically examine parity-based selection rules in semiconductor-surface states and atomic structures. Our analysis involves solving the Liouville-von Neumann equation to derive the reduced density matrix and subsequent evaluation of measurable quantities via the measure of the density matrix. Our method is applicable to tight-binding models with interactions and dephasing. We found that parity-based selection rules are generally maintained even with strong light-matter interactions, contradicting previous findings suggesting these rules break down with atomic strength exceeding the light field. Our results also indicate that the stringent conditions required for this phenomenon make it exceptionally robust. Additionally, we found that the degree of non-stationarity has a significant influence on measurable quantities in atomic structures, whereas surface states are primarily affected by the location of the atomic structures in relation to the light field.

In this context, we explore a class of holographic tensor networks called HINW, which represent a more advanced version of holographic quantum error correction codes. These networks possess two key properties: they maintain a thermal behavior similar to the holographic dual theory, and they ensure the stability of quantum information through a process called holographic dark state generation. HINW can effectively describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors, unlike their more restrictive counterparts, GWMERAs, which are only capable of depicting exponential decay patterns. Our research reveals that HINW will be particularly useful in analyzing systems within condensed matter physics, particularly those involving spatially structured scenarios, and offer a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between end-to-end correlations and the codes employed in holographic QEC.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin is conducted, focusing on a specific model incorporating norbornadiene and 9-cis beta-ionone. Calculations utilizing a vast range of parameters, including electric fields, reveal an extraordinary level of sensitivity in the reaction dynamics, with significant implications for our understanding of visual signal transduction.
